data.title: Shopify Stock Is Still Under Pressure: Is It A Buy As Valuation Concerns Persist?
data.description:
Shopify (SHOP) stock price has plunged into a bear market, moving from the October high of $181 to the current $133. It has slumped below key moving averages, a trend that continued after releasing its earnings report, which showed that its revenue growth slowed during the quarter.

Shopify’s revenue growth is slowing 

SHOP stock has plunged into a bear market, moving from a high of $180 in October to the current $133. This retreat continued after the company published its financial results, which showed that its revenue growth was slowing.

Shopify said that its revenue rose to $3.7 billion in the third quarter from $2.8 billion in the same period last year. Most of this revenue was in its merchant solutions, with the rest being in its subscription solutions.

The company's net income jumped from $264 million in the third quarter of last year to $462 million. 

However, there are signs that other parts of the business are slowing, with its global merchandise volume remaining at 30% in the last three consecutive quarters. Its European GMV dropped from 42% in the second quarter of 2024 to 33%, with the North American figure remaining at 28%.

Analysts expect the company's revenue growth will remain under pressure in the coming quarters. The average estimate among analysts is that its fourth-quarter revenue is expected to come in at $4.6 billion, up by 31.1% from the same period last year.

If the estimate is correct, the annual revenue will come in at $15.3 billion, up by 32.50% from the same period last year. This growth will then slow to 26% next year to $19.3 billion, which is quite good for a company that has been in the business for two decades.

Shopify is benefiting from the market share of its business, since it is the biggest name in the e-commerce software industry. Most recently, there is hope that it will benefit from the rise of AI agents, which are now able to shop for people. As these agents become more popular, they will lead to more shopping activity over time.

Shopify valuation concerns remains 

The main challenge facing the SHOP stock is that its business has always been highly overvalued because of its growing market share, revenue and profitability growth, and its ability to continue monetizing its products.

Shopify has a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 70, and a forward PEG multiple of 2.19. In contrast, the S&P 500 Index has a multiple of 17, while the technology median is 18.2. These numbers are also higher than other companies, including retailers like Walmart and Costco.

The only valuation multiple that can justify Shopify’s current price is the Rule-of-40, which looks at a company’s revenue growth and its margins. By adding these two numbers, Shopify has a multiple of 47%, which is higher than the key level of 40.

Analysts have a bullish outlook for the stock. Argus reiterated the buy rating and set a target of $180, while Bernstein has a target of $165. Other analysts who are bullish on the company are from Needham, Wells Fargo, and UBS Group.

Shopify stock price technical analysis 

The daily chart shows that Shopify stock has dropped sharply since mid-October, moving from a high of $180 to the current $133.

Shopify has already dropped below the ascending trendline that connects the lowest swings since May 14 this year.

The stock has also dropped below the 50-day and 200-day moving averages and is now hovering between the 50% and 61.8% Fibonacci retracement level.

Therefore, the stock will likely remain under pressure for a while and possibly retest the support at $100 and then bounce back, possibly to $150 in the future.

data.title: Tokyo Inflation Is Forecast To Jump To 3% With The Yen Under 160.00
data.description:
Tokyo's November inflation figures are forecast to jump to 3% from 2.6%, and they arrive after a call for faster rate rises failed to move the Yen for long. USD/JPY dipped to about 159.00 on a speech by Bank of Japan (BoJ) board member Tamura and is back between 159.00 and 159.50, inside Wednesday's range. It hasn't traded above 160.00 since November 13.

BoJ board member Tamura said in Kofu on Thursday that he wants the rate at about 2% as soon as possible. It is 1.25% now, and at one quarter-point rise a quarter, the fastest the BoJ has gone, 2% would arrive in June 2027, a month before his term ends. Traders put a December rise at about 71%, and the Yen's gain on the speech was gone within the session.

The gain didn't last because the rate gap is on the Dollar's side. The Fed's rate is 3.75%-4.00% against Japan's 1.25%, and the Fed is expected to raise first, on December 9. Wednesday's US figures, with growth revised up to 4.3% and core inflation at 3.3%, left USD/JPY flat as well, since Finance Minister Katayama warned against one-sided moves when the pair last crossed 160.00.

On the calendar

Tokyo's November Consumer Price Index (CPI) is due at 23:30 GMT on Thursday. The measure excluding fresh food is forecast at 3% after 2.6%, and the one excluding food and energy at 3% after 2.4%. Both feed the BoJ's December 18 decision, the Japanese side of the rate gap.

Friday is a shortened US session with nothing on the data calendar, and Fed officials go quiet from Saturday. The December 9 Fed decision is priced above 90% for a quarter-point rise, which would take the US rate to 4.00%-4.25% nine days before the BoJ decides.

On the charts

USD/JPY has recovered more than half of the drop from late July's high just under 164.00 to the September 8 low just under 153.00. Every daily close since November 10 has been above its 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA), near 158.50, and the 200-day is just under 158.00. Daily momentum has turned down from the edge of overbought.

data.title: It’s A Thanksgiving Chart Party
data.description:
Charts 1, 2, and 3: What Is This?

On Wednesday, we saw a 3% intraday round trip, a seven-point move on the VIX and the S&P 500, taking us back to flat. Not Jerome Powell was wondering what they should call this pattern. I think it should be called the… “We need to talk…”

And I call it a dream trade for Volume Weighted Average Price…

The 705 call passed VWAP at $1.31 around 11:55 am.

That was at about $13.00 two hours later.

Just saying…

It was a big move with very little participation ahead of a holiday. But it’s a reminder of what can happen when you’re patient, and the fish does bite right when you need it.

So… now we head into Friday with Goldman and other banks calling the recent runs we’ve seen “bear market action.” Well… that’s good, because we are sitting heavily in cash and looking for trading opportunities like this while our signals are negative.

Chart 4: Another Reason for the Fed to Ease?

Yesterday, I talked about the “race to cash” theme of the last week in the market.

But there’s more to it than just selling to sell and raise cash. There’s another problem: companies are absorbing cash faster than they can earn it. Next year, the capex from the big hyperscalers will surpass $1.1 trillion.

Source: JPMorgan

We know they’re well past their cash flow, which means they must borrow from banks, issue bonds that people will buy instead of stocks, and drain money from funds.

One last thing… they’re also less inclined to buy back stock.

This is all draining liquidity from the equity market…

It’s happening on a multi-month lag of up to six months.

These are the types of things that can fuel lower inflation and put the U.S. on a path back toward easing by the end of the first quarter. Recall, again, we need to refinance about $10.6 trillion at the Treasury level as well.

We still have a long way to go.

Chart 5: Forced Selling… More on Tap?

Nothing like a stock market that runs on rules, except when the rules force a level of selling in a week that surpasses the GDP of Zimbabwe.

On Wednesday, the Nasdaq 100 (QQQ) dropped 4.7%, hit bear market territory (down 20% from its peak), and then finished off just 0.6%. This sort of reversal has only happened 16 times since 1988… Again, no one can really explain all of this.

But, it feels like this became a “decline in selling” and not a big uptick in purchasing.

These types of things happen when we get to extremes where we start to experience a dramatic decline in fast-moving stocks.

There could… of course… be more selling. Goldman said trend and vol-control funds dumped $70 billion in stock… and that we could see another $100 billion this week.

Watch out for Friday. The good news is that if that selling does happen, we could finally reach a point where we can get some lower-volume bidding in early December, and into that Fed meeting. From there, I suppose we’ll just wait for the 2:35 trade.

Chart 6: When Gold Became a Risk Asset?

Gold prices aren’t trading like a haven…

Gold is trading like a risk asset.

It slumped about 9% from November 17 to 20, and then continued its downward pressure to under $3,500 yesterday. I called a local gold buyer (who appears to be overwhelmed by sellers) and he described the panic selling in the local physical market where I live as a “shit show.”

Gold has been moving with the semis, and more or less looks like an inverted dollar chart right now. Nothing is immune in a liquidation…

The one thing that I do want to note is that major desks keep talking about the 2018 cycle and will make the comparisons. But the metals are the major difference right now. Gold was up in 2018, while gold’s down 10.8% this year. The yen was strong then, and it’s week now. Copper is down 13%, more than double 2018’s decline.

So… let’s be clear here. Panic hit an extreme (and we’re in a place where a short-term bounce into the Fed meeting is plausible.) But keep in mind that a lot of funds are still protecting their gains from the year. While the capitulation from humans could be coming to a close, positioning over December will be difficult to project. Pensions will be buying stocks next week… we know this as we wrap up the month.

But is that really enough to get everyone excited to own things again?

Chart 7: Don’t Forget…

So… what comes next from the Federal Reserve?

Markets are pricing in a 25 basis point hike in December…

Source: CME Fed Watchk

We can see a 98% probability of a hike…

But there’s one thing that we should consider. Recall that Governor Waller has advocated for a 50 basis point hike… And he would be arguing for either 25 points in December and 25 in January… or 50 in December if there isn’t insight on what to expect in January.

That… by definition… makes this event a “Live Meeting.”

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh doesn’t like forward guidance, so he’s offered us none.

The desks in New York are speculating on what comes next. Several banks expect three interest rate hikes by March (I don’t really care about rate hikes when they’ll probably turn on whatever supportive policies they can in December or Q1 for the banking sector.)

That said, consumer confidence is running hot, GDP is 4.3%, and core inflation still ran hot. So, we’ll raise interest rates… at a time that growth is really driven by AI and tech spending…

Chart 8: The Thanksgiving tab.

You’ll sit down today for dinner… and probably wonder what the cost of it was…

Dinner for 10 people, according to one farm group’s annual farm survery, increased to $58.63, which was a 6.3% jump from 2025. What’s driving the hike?

Turkey costs 10% more ($23.68)…

Cranberry is up 8.8%, milk 8.6%, and dinner rolls about 7%.

One of the most important drivers in that? Diesel fuel, which is pushing $6.00 (or a 58% jump from last year).

Of course, companies like Aldi and Walmart are saying that they can do this dinner for much less… But it’s still a really good measurement of what stuff costs. Like the Chapwood Index, this survey is tracking what people really buy…

And not… the government offset numbers in tech that mask the real cost of living.

And Finally…

I want to wish everyone a very Happy Thanksgiving…

Every day it’s a joy to get up and cover the market live with everyone at Money Printer Pro… And we’ll be back tomorrow live at 8:30. So, I hope to that you enjoy the day. I wrote an article over at Eagle that reflected on wealth, and I’ll share it with you this weekend… They are publishing it first, but I want to make sure that you get a chance to see it this weekend… What real wealth is… and how to properly cherish it.

I’ll see everyone tomorrow. Happy Thanksgiving…

data.title: Open Source Vs Closed Source AI: Can Self-Hosted Models Take Revenue From Anthropic And OpenAI?
data.description:
Open source vs closed source AI decides who gets paid for the work AI does. In October 2026 Revolut said it had moved about 2,000 engineers from Claude Code to an open model on its own servers and cut its AI coding bill by roughly 90%. Across US companies, open models now process 19% of AI tokens, the pieces of words a model reads and writes, and earn 4% of the spend, so far they take work from Anthropic and OpenAI and only a small part of their revenue.

TL;DR

  1. Revolut runs GLM-5.3, an open-weight model, on 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs and reports AI coding costs about 90% lower. Amazon, Pinterest, Shopify and AT&T report cuts of 56% to 98% on narrower tasks.

  2. Open models cost US companies about 0.13 USD per million tokens against 0.70 USD for closed ones, so they gained token share while their share of spending fell to 4%.

  3. Self-hosting takes routine, high-volume work, frontier models keep the hardest tasks, and the chip and cloud suppliers earn either way.

What Is the Difference Between Open Source and Closed Source AI?

A closed source AI model stays on servers its developer chooses, its own or other companies' clouds such as AWS, and is sold per use, while an open model publishes its weights, the billions of trained numbers that make it work, so any company can download it and run it on its own hardware. Claude from Anthropic, GPT from OpenAI and Gemini from Google are closed. GLM from Z.ai (Zhipu AI), DeepSeek, Kimi from Moonshot AI and Llama from Meta are open.

Most models called open source are open weight. Their developers publish the weights and a licence and keep the training data and much of the training code to themselves. The Open Source Initiative's definition asks for enough information about the training data to rebuild the model, and few large models meet it. Licences differ too: GLM-5.1 uses the permissive MIT licence, while GLM-5.3, the version Revolut runs now, has a licence of its own.

Closed, open-weight and fully open source AI models compared

Two of the closed labs also publish open-weight models: OpenAI released gpt-oss in August 2025 and Google publishes Gemma, so one company can sell both kinds. Frontier models are the most capable models of the moment, the ones that set the top scores on benchmarks and carry the highest prices.

Why Did Revolut Move Its Engineers to an Open Model?

Revolut, the British fintech, moved about 2,000 engineers from Claude Code to GLM, an open-weight model from Z.ai, and reports AI coding costs down roughly 90%. It moved to cut a usage bill that grew with every engineer and to keep its code on hardware it controls. David Abitbol, its ops and infrastructure lead, described the change at the AI Engineer conference in New York in October 2026, as The Register reported on 3 November.

Revolut cut its AI coding bill by about 90% within a year of adopting Claude Code

  1. Early 2025. Revolut gives its engineers Gemini.

  2. Early 2026. Claude Code arrives. Some engineers spend 1,000 USD and some 10,000 USD a month before spending caps.

  3. 2026. The default becomes GLM-5.1, a 754-billion-parameter open-weight model run on Revolut's own servers at about 0.30 USD per million tokens, roughly a tenth of Claude Code or OpenAI Codex.

  4. By October 2026. GLM-5.3 serves about 2,000 engineers on 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs, seven servers of eight GPUs each.

  5. October 2026. Revolut reports AI inference costs down roughly 90%, coding time 60% better and lead time 70% better, by its own measures.

Source: The Register, 3 November 2026; TechRadar, 4 November 2026.

All of these figures come from Revolut. The bank has not published the full cost of the GPUs and of the staff who run them, so the 90% is a company estimate, and the 0.30 USD price sets an internal cost against public list prices.

Closed models stay in the setup. GLM-5.3 reads text only, so a router sends image and screen tasks to Gemini or a GPT model, and TechRadar reports that Claude Code and Codex remain available for the hardest work. Revolut cut its spending with the closed labs and kept them for the tasks where they lead.

For a regulated bank, control counts as much as price. Abitbol praised GLM for data privacy and auditability, since prompts and code stay on Revolut's own servers. PNC, one of the largest US banks, is building its own AI infrastructure and plans to use open-source models in some cases to avoid depending on vendors, American Banker reported in June 2026.

How Much Cheaper Is Open Source AI?

Per token, open models cost US companies about a fifth of what closed ones cost: an average of 0.13 USD per million tokens in September 2026 against 0.70 USD for closed models, according to the 2026 State of Enterprise AI report by Menlo Ventures, published on 3 November 2026 and based on a survey of nearly 400 enterprise decision-makers and Menlo's own market model.

List prices show the same difference. The table compares prices on the developers' own pages on 26 November 2026. Output tokens, the text a model writes, cost more than input tokens, the text it reads.

Top closed models charge nine to ten times the output price of open-weight APIs

List price per million output tokens, USD, 26 November 2026

  • Closed model

  • Open-weight model through its developer's API

List prices of seven AI models per million tokens on 26 November 2026, USD, ranked by output price

  1. Google doubles the Gemini 4 Carbon price on 1 December 2026, from 2 USD for input and 10 USD for output.

  2. Revolut runs GLM-5.1 on its own GPUs at about 0.30 USD per million tokens, input and output blended, an internal cost.

40 USD is 9.1 times GLM-5.3 and 10.1 times DeepSeek V4-Pro.

Source: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Z.ai and DeepSeek pricing pages, 26 November 2026; Revolut via The Register, 3 November 2026.

The gap is widest at the top: Claude Fable 5.2 and OpenAI's gpt-6.2-astra charge 40 USD per million output tokens, about nine times GLM-5.3 through Z.ai's own API. Google is moving the other way and doubles the price of Gemini 4 Carbon on 1 December.

Is Self-Hosted AI Cheaper Than an API?

For large teams with heavy use, yes: at Revolut's ratio, renting GPUs pays off once each engineer would spend more than about 174 USD a month on API calls. Self-hosting turns a bill per token into a bill per GPU-hour. The calculator compares the two for a team of engineers. It uses Revolut's ratio of one eight-GPU B200 server for about every 286 engineers and, by default, the median on-demand rental price of 8.50 USD per GPU-hour across 23 cloud providers on 26 November 2026, as listed by GetDeploying.

API or own servers: monthly AI bill for a team of engineers

Engineers2,000

API spend per engineer a month500 USD

B200 rental per GPU-hour8.50 USD

Monthly bill at the selected inputs

At these inputs the API bill is 1,000,000 USD a month and renting 56 B200 GPUs costs 347,480 USD, about 65.3% less. The GPUs pay off once each engineer would spend more than 174 USD a month on API calls. Staff, setup and the tasks still sent to closed models come on top of the GPU bill.

Model: one eight-GPU B200 server per 286 engineers, as at Revolut, rented around the clock for 730 hours a month. Staff, setup and the closed-model calls a router keeps are not included. The 500 USD default is our assumption: Revolut has not published its spend per engineer, and its 90% is a cut in inference costs.

A team of 100 engineers still needs a full eight-GPU server, which lifts its break-even to about 496 USD per engineer, so self-hosting suits large teams with steady, heavy use. A Futurum survey of 200 companies in October 2026 found that self-hosting costs held up half of all pilots, and only 10% of in-house builds showed a lasting return at scale.

How Close Are Open Models to Claude, GPT and Gemini?

Open models are close enough to Claude, GPT and Gemini for much routine work: in May 2026 the best open-weight models trailed the best closed ones by about four months on the capability index of Epoch AI, a research group that combines many benchmarks into one score.

A study by Frank Nagle and Daniel Yue, summarised by MIT Sloan, found that on OpenRouter, a marketplace that routes requests to many models, open models reached about 90% of closed-model performance in 2025 and switching could have cut spending by more than 70%, yet closed models kept about 80% of tokens.

Menlo Ventures' 2026 figures show where the money went. Open models gained volume, and frontier models gained more volume and most of the spending.

Open models rose to 19% of tokens and fell to 4% of spending, frontier models took 63%

Share of US enterprise AI tokens and spending, %, a year earlier and 2026

  • A year earlier

  • Open models, 2026

  • Frontier models, 2026

Share of US enterprise AI tokens and spending for open and frontier models, a year earlier and in 2026, %

Open models: September 2025 and September 2026. Frontier models: Q3 2025 and Q3 2026. Bars on one scale from 0 to 100%.

Source: Menlo Ventures, 2026: The State of Enterprise AI, 3 November 2026.

Chinese developers lead the open side. They take 89% of US enterprise spending on open models, led by Kimi with 61%, DeepSeek with 15% and GLM with 11%. Meta's Llama, the best-known American open model, has 7%. In July 2026 Fortune reported that Airbnb and Siemens were testing models from Alibaba and DeepSeek, and DoorDash's chief technology officer Andy Fang said a Moonshot AI model gave better quality at a lower cost.

Can Self-Hosted Models Replace Frontier Models?

Self-hosted and open models already replace frontier models in high-volume, well-defined tasks, while for the hardest reasoning, images and long agent tasks companies still pay for frontier models. Besides Revolut, four companies have published what moving a task to an open model saved: Amazon, Pinterest, Shopify and AT&T, as reported by The Pragmatic Engineer. Each of these covers one narrow, repeated task. The same logic runs among closed models: Siemens cut the cost of its product search by 70% with Amazon Nova 2 Lite, a smaller closed model, AWS says.

Five companies report AI costs 56% to 98% lower after moving tasks to open models

Reported cost reduction after moving one task to an open-weight model, %, as each company measures it, 2026

  • Moved to an open-weight model

Cost reduction reported by five companies after moving one task to an open-weight model in 2026, %, ranked

  1. Pinterest's CEO: cost per transaction under 8% of comparable closed models.

  2. AT&T accepted about 2% lower quality on these tasks.

Bases differ: per ticket (Amazon, 0.0005 against 0.0222 USD), per transaction (Pinterest), inference spend (Revolut), cost of coding tasks (AT&T), not stated (Shopify).

Source: Strands Agents blog, 9 November 2026; Pinterest Q2 2026 earnings call; The Register, 3 November 2026; Shopify Engineering, April 2026; The Pragmatic Engineer, September 2026.

AT&T sends about 40% of employee AI requests to open models and expects 60% to 70% within a few years, while Claude and GPT keep the harder work, executive Mark Austin told The New York Times, as summarised by AI Weekly in September 2026. Where the companies describe the setup, a router or a fixed workflow sends routine requests to the cheap model and keeps a frontier model for the rest.

Which kind of model the reported cases use for which task in 2026

Surveys point to a mixed market. Futurum found 42% of the 200 companies it asked running open-weight models in production in October 2026. A survey of 100 technology chiefs at large companies by Andreessen Horowitz in January 2026 found that preference for closed models had been rising since March 2024, with model quality, scarce AI staff and data security as the reasons.

What Does It Mean for Anthropic, OpenAI and Google Revenue?

In the near term open models press on prices and margins more than on total revenue, because enterprise AI use keeps growing and the closed labs sell the work open models cannot yet do. Menlo Ventures counts closed-model token volume up 12.1 times in a year, against 22.5 times for open models.

Menlo also tracks who gets the enterprise API money. Anthropic's share rose to 55% from 40% a year earlier, OpenAI's to 31% from 27%, and Google's fell to 9% from 21%. Menlo Ventures is an investor in Anthropic.

Anthropic gained 15 points of US enterprise API spending in a year, Google lost 12

Change in share of US enterprise LLM API spending, percentage points, a year earlier to 2026

Change in share of US enterprise LLM API spending for Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, percentage points, a year earlier to 2026

Menlo Ventures, an investor in Anthropic, estimates the shares from a survey of nearly 400 US enterprise decision-makers and its own market model.

Source: Menlo Ventures, 2026: The State of Enterprise AI, 3 November 2026.

Where open models compete with the closed labs

Menlo's blended price for closed models fell 24% in a year, and Epoch AI finds that the price of a given level of performance falls between 9 and 900 times a year, depending on the task. Anthropic had planned to raise Claude Sonnet 5 from 2 to 3 USD per million input tokens on 1 September 2026 and kept the lower price, according to its pricing page. Google is doubling the price of Gemini 4 Carbon on 1 December, so the pressure is uneven.

For Anthropic shareholders the first sign would be a lower price per token. Compute costs are a separate line, 58% of revenue in Q3 2026 against 48% in Q2, for reasons our post Is Anthropic Profitable? explains.

Which Stocks Gain When Companies Host Their Own AI?

Self-hosting moves spending from model subscriptions to chips and cloud capacity, so compute suppliers gain whichever model wins a given task: Nvidia (NVDA), which sells the GPUs, and Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet (GOOGL), which rent them out. Revolut's switch alone needed 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs.

Nvidia's data centre revenue rose 110% year on year to 107.6 billion USD in its third quarter of fiscal 2027, as covered in our Nvidia earnings post. Rental prices for the B200 rose about 24% over 90 days to a median of 8.50 USD per GPU-hour, by GetDeploying's count.

The market has read open models the other way before. On 27 January 2025, after DeepSeek showed a cheap open model close to the best closed ones, Nvidia fell about 17% in one day and lost 589 billion USD of market value, according to Bloomberg, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 3.1%. Nvidia's later results, above, show how that reading turned out.

The cloud providers host open models next to closed ones in Bedrock, Azure and Google Cloud, so they collect rent on both. Most open-model developers are private. Zhipu AI, which makes GLM under the Z.ai brand, has traded in Hong Kong as Knowledge Atlas Technology (HKEX: 2513) since 8 January 2026.

Will Open Models Become One of the Main AI Trends?

By volume open models are already a main AI trend: open-weight token use across US companies grew 22.5 times in a year, according to Menlo Ventures. The money follows more slowly, because companies pay most for the hardest work and frontier models still do it best.

Software has gone through a similar split. Linux, a free operating system, came to run most of the world's servers, and software vendors kept growing by selling what customers would not build themselves. AI looks set to divide the same way: open models for high-volume routine work, closed models for the hardest tasks and a router between them, as at Revolut.

Five signals will show how fast the balance moves:

  1. Anthropic's first quarterly reports as a public company: revenue growth and compute costs as a share of revenue, 58% in Q3 2026.

  2. The next Menlo Ventures survey: whether open models' 4% share of enterprise spending starts to rise.

  3. New company cases with cost figures, beyond the companies above, and whether any of them moves harder work than coding, sorting and support.

  4. Prices at the top: whether Anthropic and OpenAI follow Google's price rise or keep cutting.

  5. Nvidia's data centre revenue in its next quarterly report.

Conclusion

Open source vs closed source AI is turning into a split by task. Open models already handle a fifth of US enterprise AI tokens at about a fifth of the price, and companies from Revolut to Amazon report cutting the cost of routine tasks by 56% to 98% after moving them. The closed labs still take most of the money, and frontier models raised their share of enterprise spending from 35% to 63% in a year.

For investors the switch weighs first on the price per token at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, while revenue keeps growing: Anthropic's rose 47% from Q2 to Q3 2026. Chip and cloud suppliers gain from both kinds of model, and Nvidia's data centre revenue of 107.6 billion USD last quarter shows the size of that demand.

data.title: Mag 7 Weekly: Jensen Is Back. The Cash Question Is Not.
data.description:
This Mag 7 week had one plot twist and a hangover. Nvidia (NVDA) put Jensen Huang back in the CEO chair after less than two weeks away, and the stock ripped more than 30% on Monday. That was the best single day for Nvidia since 2003 and about $950 billion of market value in one session. Then the same AI credit and buildout fears that crushed the group into last Friday came right back on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Through the last regular close before Thanksgiving, Apple (AAPL) was the only Mag 7 name green on the week, up about 0.9% near $356. Amazon (AMZN) took the worst week near minus 9% on AI spending stress. Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOGL), Meta (META), Nvidia, and Tesla (TSLA) all finished slightly red to soft after the bounce faded. Markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving, so this board is the week that counts for the Mag 7 send.

Apple still owns the year near plus 31%. Nvidia is still down about 21% year to date even after Monday's rocket ride. The story is not "AI is dead." The story is who can fund the buildout without scaring the people who buy the bonds and the stock.

The Scoreboard

Prices and moves as of the Wednesday, November 25 regular close. U.S. markets closed Thursday for Thanksgiving.

Jensen Walks Back In. The Market Still Wants Receipts.

Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as president, chief executive, and director effective immediately after he stepped down following media reports about his personal life, including contact questions that pulled in national-security headlines. President Trump said he pushed the board to bring Huang back. Huang said he was honored to return at the start of what he called a new industrial revolution.

Monday priced the relief. Nvidia closed near $165, up about 31% from Friday's roughly $126 low, after trading even higher intraday. Chip names and AI infrastructure names ripped with it. By Tuesday the bounce cooled. By Wednesday Nvidia was back in the red for the session, closing near $149, still roughly flat on the five-day board and still down more than 30% over the past month and about 21% on the year.

My take is blunt. The market can celebrate the founder walking back through the door. It will not forget the harder questions that were already on the table before the scandal: how much AI spending is funded with real free cash, how much sits on borrowed money, and whether custom chips from the hyperscalers chip away at Nvidia's grip. Leadership drama made the week violent. Cash and credit still decide the next chapter.

Apple Holds. Amazon Gets Hit. Microsoft Goes Code Red.

Apple (AAPL) closed near $356, up about 0.9% on the week and still the clear Mag 7 year-to-date leader near plus 31%. When AI names catch fire and then smoke, money still treats Apple more like a cash machine than a pure data-center buildout bet. That insulation is why Apple can look boring on a Huang Monday and still win the year.

Amazon (AMZN) had the ugliest Mag 7 week, down about 8.7% to roughly $244. The pressure was the same story investors keep circling: huge AI and cloud capital plans meeting higher funding costs and louder doubt about how fast those dollars turn into profit. Amazon is still positive on the year near plus 8%, but this week it paid the bill for being tied to the buildout trade.

Microsoft (MSFT) finished near $490, down about 3.6% on the week. The company news that stuck was operational, not a product launch. After a roughly 24-hour Microsoft 365 outage earlier this month that hit Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, internal memos described a Code Red push to fix how Microsoft prevents and recovers from major failures. Satya Nadella already apologized publicly. Reliability is not a side story when governments, airlines, and trading desks sit on your cloud.

Alphabet, Meta, and Tesla

Alphabet (GOOGL) closed near $273, down about 3.3% on the week and still soft on the month near minus 15%. Wednesday's session tagged fresh lows for the name before it bounced off the worst levels as AI-linked credit fears hit hyperscalers and chip suppliers together. Meta (META) finished near $610 after a solid Wednesday bounce, still slightly red on the week and negative year to date near minus 6%. Tesla (TSLA) closed near $380, roughly flat to soft on the week near minus 1%. SpaceX combination talk and Cybercab autonomy-fee headlines kept the story moving, but Tesla still sits about 13% under water on the year.

Bottom Line

Jensen Huang is back. That removed one giant unknown for Nvidia and lit the whole AI complex for a day. It did not erase the credit scare, the capex bill, or the split inside the Mag 7. Apple still leads the year because the market trusts its cash engine. Amazon took the week's worst hit. Microsoft has to prove the cloud stays up. Next week the same test stays on the table: who turns AI spend into cash you can count, and who is just running on hope and borrowed time.

data.title: EUR-USD: Peak Seasonality At Year-End
data.description:
Today I’m showing you one of my favorite seasonal patterns. It’s about the US dollar, and I’ll present it to you using the euro-dollar currency pair.

Why is it one of my favorite patterns? I prefer time windows of at least a week, preferably longer. As a quantitative trading system developer, I have not managed to program a stable system for the forex market in this time window.

There are exceptions, though, and seasonality provides them, especially the one at year-end.

So let’s take a look at the seasonal path of the euro against the US dollar.

The seasonal path of the euro-dollar pair in detail

The seasonal chart shows you the typical seasonal path of the euro against the US dollar. It was calculated from the average of returns over the past 26 years. The horizontal axis shows the point in the year, the vertical axis the level of the seasonal index. This way, you can see at a glance how the US dollar moves through the course of the year.

Euro against the US dollar, seasonal path, calculated over 26 years

Seasonally, the euro rises sharply ahead of the turn of the year. Source: Seasonax | View data

As you can see, the euro rises seasonally toward the end of the year. It is the strongest seasonal move of the year. After that, it weakens again. What do the results look like in detail?

Win rate: 73,1 percent

The bar chart shows you the return of the euro against the US dollar over the past 26 years in the period between November 23 and December 20. In blue you see the years in which there were gains, in red those in which losses occurred.

Euro against the US dollar, return in percent between November 23 and December 20, in individual years since 2000

Most of the time, it went up. Source: Seasonax | View data

In 19 of the 26 cases, the euro rose during this phase at the turn of the year, with most of the losing years falling between 2007 and 2016. The average return was 1.9 percent, the annualized return 20.2 percent. Given the low volatility of currencies, that is quite a lot, as the seasonal chart already suggested.

The euro has only existed since the turn of the millennium. Other currencies, however, have existed much longer. They, too, show a comparable strength against the dollar at the turn of the year, going back as far as the 1970s. What is the reason for that?

The reason for the US dollar’s year-end slump

The rise of currencies against the dollar corresponds to a decline of the US dollar against those currencies. Since the phenomenon also occurs with other currencies, it is a phenomenon of the US dollar itself.

The US dollar’s reversal at the turn of the year is already a hint as to the reason for this seasonal pattern: it should be connected to the calendar year-end. And what happens at year-end? The balance sheet date!

The decline of the US dollar toward year-end is rooted in American tax law. Many American companies save on taxes by reporting the lowest possible amounts on the balance sheet date at year-end. In that case, it can be worthwhile to transfer funds to the accounts of foreign subsidiaries.

The additional demand for foreign currencies that this creates does not go without consequences for the exchange rate. That is why the US dollar typically falls toward year-end, while the euro and other currencies rise.

After the turn of the year, the tide turns. Companies transfer much of the funds back again, and the US dollar typically rises, while the euro and other currencies fall.

data.title: Oil Price Today: Brent Edges Up After Fresh Tanker Attacks Near Strait Of Hormuz
data.description:
Oil price today is edging higher after the UK's maritime security agency confirmed a tanker was hit by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran claimed two more tankers struck mines nearby.

Brent futures for February delivery, the most actively traded contract, were up $0.66, or 0.7%, at $91.30 a barrel at 16:25 UK time. That compares with Wednesday's settlement of $90.64.

US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) for January was up $1.14, or 1.4%, at $84.82.

With US markets shut for Thanksgiving, trading is thinner than usual.

What happened in Strait of Hormuz?

UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) published Warning 223-26 on Thursday, classifying the incident as an attack.

It said local authorities had reported that an outbound tanker was struck by an unknown projectile 18 nautical miles east of Khasab, Oman, at 13:00 UK time on Wednesday, November 25. The crew has been accounted for and there is no report of environmental impact.

A separate UKMTO warning said a tanker's master reported an explosion from an unknown projectile close to the vessel 50 nautical miles west of Dubai at 21:30 UK time on Wednesday. No damage was reported.

That followed Warning 221-26, which reported a tanker struck by a projectile in the strait on Sunday. UKMTO has not named any of the ships or said who fired.

What is Iran claiming?

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said two tankers "in violation of regulations" hit naval mines north of Khasab in the early hours of Thursday, according to a statement carried by Iran's Tasnim news agency.

It said one was a supertanker carrying more than 2M barrels of crude that was "left burning". The IRGC said the tankers had switched off their navigation systems and were using an unauthorised route.

Those claims have not been independently confirmed. No vessel has been named, and UKMTO had not issued a warning matching the IRGC's account by the time of writing.

Separately, Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery, causing fires.

The Saudi-led coalition said air defences destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura but did not say the refinery was hit, Al Jazeera reported.

Why is oil price not rising more?

February Brent climbed from a morning low of $89.75 at 09:20 UK time to about $91 by 11:00 UK time, after the IRGC statement was first reported.

It has not regained its day high of $92.08, touched at 05:40 UK time.

That leaves Brent well short of a 3% daily move. Traders have watched repeated attacks on Gulf shipping this month, and prices have fallen despite fresh incidents.

The two-day picture is firmer. February Brent is up 2.8% from Tuesday's settlement of $88.78.

The expiring January Brent contract, which stops trading on Monday, was at $96.00, a premium of $4.70 to February. A steep premium for the nearest month usually points to tight prompt supply.

Brent chart | Source: ICE via TradingView

What happens next for oil prices?

OPEC+ ministers meet on Sunday, November 29. The 42nd OPEC and non-OPEC Ministerial Meeting was set in June, and the seven OPEC+ countries that review output monthly also meet that day.

Any change to supply policy could matter more for prices than a single tanker incident. Production baselines for 2027 are on the agenda.

In the Gulf, the key test is whether UKMTO or the ship owners confirm the IRGC's mine claims. A confirmed hit on a fully laden supertanker would be a bigger supply story.

Thursday's low of $89.75 and high of $92.08 are the near-term levels to watch on February Brent.

Oil is caught between rising security risks in the Gulf and expectations of a supply surplus next year. That mix can trigger sharp moves in either direction, especially in thin holiday trade.

data.title: Black Friday Stocks Come With Prices, They Don’t Necessarily Come With Discounts
data.description:
Black Friday stock market hours in 2026 give investors a shorter session, not an automatic bargain. Retailers can advertise discounts. Your brokerage account still requires you to determine whether the price makes sense.

NYSE cash-equity markets close at 1 p.m. Eastern on Friday, November 27. Eligible options close at 1:15 p.m. Certain NYSE venues operate late sessions until 5 p.m., according to the exchange group’s holiday calendar.

Before placing an order, confirm your broker’s schedule and the security’s trading session. An exchange’s published hours do not guarantee your account supports every available session.

A Short Session Does Not Predict Every Stock’s Liquidity

It is tempting to describe every holiday session as dangerously thin. That conclusion requires evidence about the security and trading conditions, rather than the date alone.

A heavily traded stock can still offer competitive quotes. Another security can display limited depth or a wide spread. Examine the live market instead of assuming all shares behave identically.

The shortened schedule does create a practical deadline. Investors expecting an ordinary afternoon session could discover their intended trading window has already closed. A calendar check costs considerably less than an avoidable mistake.

The Last Price Is Not Your Guaranteed Price

A stock’s last transaction shows where an earlier trade occurred. It does not promise the price available for your next order.

For example, a hypothetical stock last traded at $50. Its current best bid could be $49.90 and its best offer $50.10. Buying immediately near the offer and selling immediately near the bid would create a $0.20 difference before other costs.

On 1,000 shares, that difference represents $200. Commission-free trading has not made arithmetic disappear.

Quotes change, and execution can receive price improvement. The example illustrates the spread rather than predicting a particular fill.

Market Orders Prioritize Execution

A market order seeks execution at available prices. Investor.gov explains that its execution price is not guaranteed. Fast price changes or limited available shares can produce a result different from the quote an investor recently saw.

Order size matters alongside the displayed price. The best offer might cover fewer shares than you intend to purchase. Additional shares can execute at different prices as the order reaches available sellers.

This does not make every market order inappropriate. It means investors should understand which objective they prioritize: immediate execution or a defined price boundary.

Limit Orders Set a Boundary, Not an Appointment

A buy limit order specifies the highest acceptable purchase price. A sell limit order specifies the lowest acceptable sale price. Execution can occur at the limit or better, but a fill is not assured.

A hypothetical investor seeking 200 shares with a $50 buy limit will not accept a fill above $50 under that instruction. If sellers remain above the limit, the investor could receive no shares.

Even a trade occurring at the limit does not guarantee every waiting order fills. Available quantity and order priority matter. Price control comes with the possibility of missing the trade.

Check Duration and Cancellation Instructions

A day order and a good-til-canceled order have different lifespans. Broker policies also determine whether an instruction applies to regular trading, extended trading, or both.

Review those settings before submission. Do not assume an unfilled order will remain active through the session you intended.

After requesting cancellation, check the order status. A cancellation request does not establish that an order stopped before execution. Placing a replacement without confirming the original status can create an unintended additional position.

A shorter day rewards preparation. It does not reward hurried clicking.

Extended Hours Require Separate Attention

Trading after the early cash-session close is different from trading during the shortened regular session. Broker access, eligible securities, and accepted order types vary.

The SEC’s extended-hours bulletin identifies risks including reduced liquidity, wider spreads and differing prices across trading venues. These observations concern extended trading and should not be automatically applied to every regular-session Black Friday trade.

Check current quotes, the session designation and your broker’s rules. Additional access provides another opportunity to trade. It does not independently establish an attractive execution opportunity.

The Calendar Does Not Replace Valuation

A stock falling during a holiday session is not necessarily undervalued. A stock rising is not necessarily becoming a better investment.

Separate your business thesis from the mechanics of entering the position. Decide what you want to own, why you want it and which price supports your expected return. Then evaluate execution.

NYSE’s early close supplies a deadline. It supplies no requirement to complete a trade.

Check the clock, spread, size, and order settings. Black Friday advertising already creates enough urgency. Your portfolio does not need to participate.

AI contributes the lion’s share of the change in real private fixed investment, currently 89.43 percent.

From the above percentages and the BEA published contributions to GDP we can calculate the AI percentage point contribution to GDP.

The AI percentage point contribution to GDP = AI-Related Percent of the change in Real Private Fixed Investment * the BEA published Private Nonresidential Contribution (yellow bars below).

AI Percentage Point Contribution to GDP

For 2026 Q3, the BEA says GDP rose 4.3 percent.

The private nonresidental contribution to GDP was 2.2 percentage points of which 89.43 percent (2.0 percentage point) was AI related.

Thus, AI contributed 2.0 percentage points to that overall 4.3 percent.

But that’s not the best way of looking at things. GDP includes CIPI (Change in Private Inventories) that net to zero over time.

Real Final Sales subtracts CIPI and is the best bottom line GDP number. The following chart shows AI contribution to GDP and Real Final Sales.

AI Percent of Real GDP and Real Final Sales

AI Contribution to Real GDP and Real Final Sales

  • 2025 Q1: Undefined

  • 2025 Q2: 37.4% and 20.2%

  • 2025 Q3: 17.8% and 17.4%

  • 2025 Q4: 520.4% and 346.9%

  • 2026 Q1: 77.4% and 84.1%

  • 2026 Q2: 37.7% and 29.7%

  • 2026 Q3: 46.2% and 76.4%

Negative numbers make 2025 Q1 comparisons undefined.

Small numbers make 2025 Q4 contributions look ridiculous. So let’s discuss 2026.

AI-related expenses accounted for approximately 54 percent of GDP and 63 percent of real final sales so far in 2026.

Two Key Questions

  1. How sustainable is the AI growth?

  2. How much of the AI expenditure is malinvestment that will be written off?

We know the answer to the first question. It’s not. The answer to the second question is problematic.

Logically, I view GDP as overstated by the amount of malinvestment. But we don’t know the amount yet.

And no one ever subtracts malinvestment when the writeoffs do happen. Instead, malinvestment and writeoffs will eventually subtract from future growth.

Bombing the Desert

As with private malinvestment, government spending, no matter how useless or counterproductive adds to GDP.

data.title: Three Washington Changes Traders Should Watch In 2027
data.description:
Several developments in Washington caught my attention this week, including the final results of the midterm elections, a change to the Federal Reserve’s meeting schedule, and new nominations to the agencies overseeing financial markets.

Each has different implications for 2027, and some are more relevant to our trading than others.

Democrats have secured control of both chambers of Congress, creating a divided government with President Donald Trump in the White House. However, their Senate majority will remain below the 60 votes generally needed to overcome a filibuster on most legislation.

That could limit major changes to tax and spending policies without bipartisan agreement. For businesses, the implications depend on which proposals advance. Corporate tax changes would affect after-tax earnings, while federal spending decisions could influence revenue in industries that rely heavily on government contracts.

A divided government could also leave existing policies in place longer than anticipated. Until specific legislation develops, the election results offer limited information about the direction of stock prices.

The Federal Reserve announced a more unusual change. Beginning in 2027, the Fed plans to hold eight meetings per year, but vote on interest rates at only seven. Its October meeting will focus on longer-term monetary policy strategy, with plans to reduce the number of rate-setting meetings further in 2028.

We’ve discussed inflation and interest rate expectations recently, but the new schedule introduces another consideration.

With fewer scheduled decisions, there could be longer intervals between opportunities for the Fed to formally adjust rates. Economic conditions and market expectations will continue changing during those periods, potentially increasing attention on the remaining policy meetings.

The Fed retains the ability to act between scheduled meetings, so fewer votes don ’t necessarily mean greater volatility. The significance will depend on how policymakers communicate and respond as economic conditions develop.

Financial regulation is another area worth following. President Trump has nominated four commissioners to fill vacancies at the SEC and CFTC. The SEC oversees securities markets, including the stock options we trade, while the CFTC primarily regulates futures and related derivatives.

Additional commissioners could allow the agencies to advance regulatory decisions. For our options strategy, changes to clearing practices, market structure, or margin requirements would be relevant because they could affect trading costs or capital requirements. The nominations themselves do not change those conditions.

The SEC has also proposed reducing executive compensation disclosures, including limiting mandatory reporting to CEOs and CFOs. Although the changes could lower compliance costs, they would also reduce information available about compensation for other senior executives. The implications are more relevant to evaluating individual companies than to the broader market.

Of these developments, the Fed’s revised schedule is the most immediate change to an established process. The economic consequences of divided government and new regulatory appointments will depend on decisions still ahead.

Fortunately, my volatility indicator doesn’t require us to forecast those outcomes. It is designed to identify opportunities across different market environments, using consistent signals and risk management rules.

Trump Turns to Section 301 Tariffs

The New York Times reports Trump Administration Unveils New Tariffs for Dozens of Countries, Citing Unfair Practices

The Trump administration proposed a slate of new tariffs on Wednesday targeting imports from dozens of countries, including China, Japan and the members of the European Union, marking the latest expansion of a global trade war that faces mounting obstacles in Congress and the courts.

The administration framed the duties as a response to unfair trade practices, as it accused some of its closest economic partners of overproducing certain products, undercutting American businesses and contributing to a swelling U.S. trade deficit.

The newly unveiled roster of tariffs included a 20 percent tax on some imports from China, which the Trump administration signaled it could ratchet up — to 40 percent — if Beijing does not hew to the terms of a trade truce it has struck with Washington.

The Trump administration also proposed similarly high and potentially escalating rates on goods from the 27 members of the European Union and other trading partners including Cambodia, India, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam. Some of those duties could reach up to 20 percent as well. And it coupled the sweeping action with a separate, specific proposal seeking to raise rates on Brazil, targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.

Before the new tariffs take effect, the administration must fulfill a set of final regulatory requirements, which would include seeking public feedback, according to Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, who appeared Wednesday on CNBC. He described the approach as “targeted,” but noted that discussions continued with each of the affected trading partners.

In many cases, though, Mr. Greer said the tariffs would not stack on top of those that the administration had already put in place. That included duties that President Trump has applied on national security grounds to products such as steel and cars. He said the White House also sought to keep its tariffs in line with the trade agreements it had already brokered.

The battery of new tariffs nonetheless arrived at a precarious political moment for Mr. Trump, who has continued to engage in a strategy of aggressive trade brinkmanship even after the Supreme Court struck down his initial slate of country-by-country duties this year.

The announcement also appeared to rankle the country’s closest allies and trading partners. Some had already struck deals with Mr. Trump to avert higher tariffs — or were in the midst of negotiations — when the administration signaled Wednesday that it could raise rates even higher.

Mr. Trump’s newly proposed tariffs on the European Union would be set at 15 percent, as the agreement between trans-Atlantic partners had stipulated. But the administration also warned it could raise rates as high as 25 percent if it found compliance was “unsatisfactory.”

Terrible Time for New Tariffs

The Wall Street Journal reports Why This Is a Terrible Time for New Tariffs

Given their unpopularity, there is never a good time to raise tariffs. That said, this week was especially bad.

The Trump administration announced a new round of tariff increases Wednesday at the same time a key measure of inflation reached a three-year high—and mere weeks after Republicans were crushed in a midterm election that turned on affordability.

The tariffs will take effect after a comment period scheduled to end Jan. 5 and hearing scheduled for Jan. 25. The aggregate impact on inflation is likely to be modest; the U.S. Trade Representative said they incorporate, rather than stack on top of, existing duties and won’t exceed previously agreed caps in deals negotiated with trading partners like the European Union.

The Budget Lab at Yale University estimates the new levies would lift the average effective tariff for the U.S. from 11.4% to 13.9%, close to the rate that prevailed before the February Supreme Court ruling. The group, founded by former Biden administration economists, estimates they could raise consumer prices by 0.3%.

Fed governor Chris Waller earlier this month said firms will raise prices if they think consumers can handle it: “I heard it just last week talking to somebody, ‘Man, we put through 3% because we think we can get it.’ And that’s when you start having problems of trying to get inflation down.”

San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said, “Increasingly we’re hearing businesses say, ‘I’m at the end of my line. I’m going to have to pass some of these input costs through.’”

This simply proves how visceral and unshakable Trump’s attachment is to tariffs. He certainly isn’t doing it for the financial or political rewards.

Pall Over Thanksgiving

Bloomberg reports Trump’s Tariffs Cast New Pall Over Thanksgiving

The debates around the supper table this year offer little to relax about. The invincible stock market suddenly seems wobbly and the data center frenzy — a pillar of the current expansion — shows cracks. Washington is gripped with talk of AI fears, spy scandals, corruption probes and pardons.

Two distant wars grind on. Interest rates look to go higher just before Christmas.

And in perhaps the most curiously timed policy move in either of his administrations, President Donald Trump’s new tariffs announced yesterday would make imports more expensive.

Americans are closer to the beginning than the end of rising food costs. Prices are also surging for generators and toilet paper after a series of tech failures spooked the public into stockpiling survival items.

Tone Deaf Economic Illiterate

Trump is a tone deaf economic illiterate, to put things politely.

It is indisputable that tariffs raise prices and cost jobs. And the election speaks for itself, except to MAGA republicans who still salute their moron-in-chief.

Trump believes Republicans lost the election because he was not on the ballot. Instead, it was a blowout precisely because voters acted like Trump was on the ballot.

It’s a “savagely brutal map” for Republicans in 2028. Meanwhile, Trump is Trump.

data.title: Gold At Record Highs Is Not An Inflation Story. It Is A Trust Story.
data.description:
For three years running, central banks have bought more than 1,000 tonnes of gold annually, according to the World Gold Council. That is roughly double the average pace of the 2010s, and it has continued through rate cuts, rate hikes, a strong dollar and a weak one. When the official sector buys that consistently, retail sentiment stops being the driver. Something structural is underneath.

The standard explanation is inflation. It does not fit. Inflation in the major economies has fallen sharply from its 2022 peak, yet gold kept making record highs. Real yields, the old enemy of gold, stayed positive and high by historical standards, and gold rallied anyway. The correlations that governed the metal for two decades have broken, one after another.

What changed in 2022 was not consumer prices. It was the weaponization of reserves. When roughly $300 billion of Russian central bank assets were frozen, every reserve manager in the world learned the same lesson: a reserve asset is only yours if the issuer lets you keep it. Treasuries are safe in a market sense. They are not safe in a political sense. Gold has no issuer. That single property, irrelevant for forty years, is now being priced.

Look at who is buying. The National Bank of Poland, the People's Bank of China, the central banks of India, Turkey, and a rotating cast of emerging markets. These are not momentum traders. They are institutions with thirty-year horizons, and they are swapping paper claims on other governments for metal in their own vaults. The share of the dollar in disclosed global reserves has slid from above 70 percent at the turn of the century to the high 50s, per IMF COFER data (data.imf.org). Nobody is dumping dollars. They are simply hedging the system that produced them.

There is a second engine: debt. US federal debt is above $36 trillion and rising by roughly $2 trillion a year, with interest costs now rivaling the defense budget. Japan, Britain and France have their own versions. Bond markets can absorb a lot, but the question has shifted from "will these debts be repaid" to "in what currency, worth how much." Gold is the asset that asks that question loudest.

What does this mean for the price? Official-sector demand does not chase. It accumulates on weakness and ignores strength, which builds a floor under corrections. As long as reserve diversification continues, dips get bought by someone with deeper pockets and a longer clock than any hedge fund.

The risks to the view are real. A genuine peace dividend, a credible sanctions rollback, or a long stretch of high real yields with a calm geopolitical map would slow official buying. Gold also pays nothing, and when the premium for safety shrinks, opportunity cost returns. Watch the quarterly central bank demand data more than the daily fix; that is the tell.

But the bigger point stands. Gold is not signaling that your groceries will cost more next year. It is signaling that the plumbing of the international monetary system is being rebuilt with more redundancy and less trust. Investors who treat the rally as a bubble are fighting the one class of buyer that never has to sell.

This is analysis, not investment advice. Do your own research.

data.title: The World’s Most Valuable Semiconductor Companies In 2026
data.description:
Inside the World’s $15 Trillion

Key Takeaways

  • Nvidia alone accounts for roughly a quarter of the combined market value of the world’s semiconductor companies.

  • Just three companies, Nvidia, TSMC, and Broadcom, are collectively worth $7.3 trillion.

  • Asian semiconductor companies account for roughly a third of the industry’s combined market capitalization.

The global race for computing power has created some of the most valuable businesses in history. From AI processors to advanced manufacturing equipment, semiconductor companies now have a combined market capitalization of over $15 trillion.

This graphic visualizes the world’s most valuable semiconductor companies using November 2026 data from CompaniesMarketCap.

The dataset includes publicly traded chipmakers, equipment suppliers, and software companies. Diversified businesses such as Samsung and Broadcom are valued in full, including their non-semiconductor operations.

The Big Three Semiconductor Companies

The three most valuable semiconductor companies specialize in different parts of the computing ecosystem: Nvidia designs powerful processors, TSMC manufactures advanced chips, and Broadcom supplies custom silicon and networking technology.

Nvidia, the world’s most valuable semiconductor company, has a market capitalization of $3.8 trillion, more than the combined value of TSMC ($2 trillion) and Broadcom ($1.6 trillion).

The table below ranks major semiconductor companies by market capitalization in November 2026, with smaller companies grouped by geography.

Nvidia’s competitive position extends beyond its processors. The company’s extensive software libraries help developers build applications for AI, scientific computing, and other demanding workloads. This combination makes its hardware part of a broader computing ecosystem.

Fellow American company Broadcom benefits from a different part of the same investment boom: custom AI accelerators and networking. Its AI semiconductor revenue reached $16.7 billion in its third fiscal quarter of 2026, up 221% from a year earlier.

Asia: The World’s Manufacturing Center

While American companies lead the industry by market capitalization, much of the world’s advanced chip manufacturing depends on Asian businesses.

Taiwan’s TSMC leads the region by market value, followed by South Korea’s Samsung ($967.1 billion) and SK hynix ($596 billion). These companies occupy critical positions in the global supply chain, from processor manufacturing to advanced memory.

Unlike Samsung, TSMC focuses on manufacturing customers’ chip designs rather than selling competing chips under its own brand. This allows rival chip designers to rely on the same manufacturing specialist.

Memory is another critical ingredient. AI processors need rapid access to enormous quantities of data, driving demand for high-bandwidth memory. This helps explain the high valuations of memory suppliers such as SK hynix.

Europe’s Crucial Role

European companies account for less than 10% of the industry’s combined market capitalization. Yet one Dutch company supplies technology that much of the world’s advanced chip manufacturing depends on.

ASML ($548.3 billion), Europe’s most valuable company, is the world’s only manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems. These machines use light to print the exceptionally fine patterns needed to produce leading-edge semiconductors.

The geographic distribution of market value tells only part of the story. While the U.S. captures the largest share of the industry’s market capitalization, the technology behind those valuations depends on specialized companies across the globe.

data.title: The United States Of Silicon Valley
data.description:
On Monday morning a little before 9am EST, the unthinkable happened: despite being under investigation for illegally evading a US Export Ban on exporting certain NVDA chips to China, Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia.

What happened?

In an interview with CNBC Monday morning, it became clear that President Trump played an instrumental role in having Huang reinstated. As the AI complex continued to unravel, sending the stock market into a tailspin, Trump sought to put a stop to it. Re-installing Huang, despite mounting evidence that he violated the Export Ban, seemed like the best way to do it. “The response from the market has been very positive. That really shows the decision was right,” Trump said Monday evening in an interview with the WSJ.

But does it?

John Adams famously said that a republic is “an empire of laws, not of men.” That means that it’s not about who you know or who you are. Everybody has to play by the same rules that are thought to best promote the flourishing of the country. The rationale behind the Export Ban is to prevent China, our enemy, from having the most powerful NVDA chips that would help them develop advanced AI that could be deployed by their military against US citizens and strategic interests. In other words, Trump sold out America to prop up the stock market.

In strong arming the Nvidia board to reinstall Huang, Trump brushed aside Huang’s intentional flouting of the Export Ban to send high level NVDA chips to China, some of which have almost certainly ended up in the hands of the Chinese military and could some day be used against the United States and its interests militarily, because of Huang’s central importance to the AI complex and therefore the economy and stock market as a whole. Patriots were outraged while the Silicon Valley elite breathed a sigh of relief as the move reinvigorated NVDA stock – and their portfolios.

From a political and ethical perspective, Trump’s intervention is illegal and despicable. After being a Trump supporter for ten years, I can no longer support a man who claims to want to “Make America Great Again” but is willing to sell out the country in order to prop up a falling stock market that threatened his popularity and political clout. He did the wrong thing for the country’s long term interests in order to shore up his own political standing and power.

It may not even work. While NVDA stock rallied hard on Monday morning, it sold off most of the rest of the day as well as Tuesday and Wednesday. It failed to reclaim the level at which it closed the day before Huang resigned as CEO (Huang resigned as CEO on Thursday November 12; NVDA stock closed at $173.73 on Wednesday November 11).

That’s because the stock market at some level knows that this was a rotten deal and that the President’s “pardon” of Huang doesn’t make all the dirty laundry go away. Facts continue to emerge about Huang’s shady dealings with Singapore shell companies, including Megaspeed, the one led by the alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang he was having an affair with, to illegally smuggle advanced NVDA chips to China (for what could already be pieced together on the morning of Monday November 16, see my “The Smoking Gun Against Jensen Huang and NVDA”).

In fact, my bet is that while this wager has propped up the market in the short term, it only delays and will make the inevitable unwinding that much worse. As brilliant and talented an entrepreneur as Jensen Huang is, when you put someone above the law simply because he is powerful, you undermine the long term fabric of a country that is great because it is a nation of laws, not of men.

The rule of law is what historically distinguishes the United States from all the autocracies in which dictators change the rules of the game to suit them as they go along. If you think this was the right move simply because the stock market went up in the short term, you’re placing way too much value on the opinion of Wall Street – and the Silicon Valley – about what really matters. Wall Street would gladly sell out the country for a quick trillion – and that’s all the stock market reaction means.
