data.title: How Spain’s Parties Plan To Raise Incomes As Low Earners Gain Ground
data.description:
Spain's monthly pay rose faster at the bottom than across much of the middle, though the largest gains were concentrated near the top. The political parties differ on how to raise incomes. Some favour a higher minimum wage and shorter working hours; others emphasise tax cuts and hiring incentives, or propose deregulation and tighter access to benefits

Between 2023 and 2025, average gross monthly pay rose by 10% in Spain’s lowest wage decile, compared with around 7% to 8% across deciles two to six. The three highest deciles recorded gains of 11% to 12%.

Over the longer period from 2019, the bottom decile recorded the strongest pay growth. Average gross monthly pay rose by about 33%, compared with 23% in the fifth decile and 27% in the top decile. Spain’s sharp minimum-wage increases are likely to have supported earnings near the bottom, although these figures cannot isolate their effect. Workers move between deciles, while changes in hours worked, occupation and seniority also affect average monthly pay.

Wage growth has been strongest at the bottom and top

Change in average gross monthly wage by overall wage decile, 2023-2025 (%)

Source: INE, ING Economic Research

Faster growth has not removed the large differences in pay. In 2025, employees in the lowest overall wage decile earned an average of €709 per month, compared with €1,970 in the fifth decile and €5,983 in the 10th.

With Spain voting on 29 November, the election programmes offer three different approaches to raising household incomes. The Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) wants to continue raising statutory wages, reduce working time and expand social support. Partido Popular places more weight on tax relief, incentives for stable employment and refundable family benefits. Vox proposes broader tax cuts, less labour regulation and tighter eligibility rules for social assistance.

Low monthly wages also reflect limited working hours

Monthly earnings depend on working time as well as wage rates. In 2025, 86.3% of employees in the lowest monthly-wage decile worked part-time. The share fell to 32.2% in the second decile and to around 9.5% and 7.5% in the third and fourth deciles, respectively. Part-time employment was uncommon from the middle of the distribution onward.

Temporary contracts followed a similar, though less extreme, pattern. They accounted for 32.7% of employees in the first decile and 18.9% in the second, compared with 3.9% in the top decile. Employees with a foreign nationality represented more than one-fifth of the first three deciles: 20.9%, 24.5%, and 25.0%, respectively.

Part-time and temporary work are concentrated in lower wage deciles

Share of employees in each overall wage decile, 2025 (%)

Source: INE, ING Economic Research

These figures put the minimum wage debate into perspective. A higher wage floor can raise hourly or full-time-equivalent pay, but it cannot guarantee enough paid hours. Someone working a short or irregular schedule can remain on a low monthly income even when the statutory rate rises. Contract stability, predictable schedules and access to full-time work therefore matter alongside the wage floor.

The programmes rely on different combinations of wage regulation, working-time rules, tax reductions, cash benefits and public services.

PSOE would continue the wage-led approach

PSOE would continue using the minimum wage as part of a broader labour market strategy. Since 2018, the monthly rate has risen from €736 to €1,221, paid 14 times a year. The programme would place the minimum wage above 60% of the average wage in law, with future adjustments reflecting prices, wages, productivity and workers’ needs.

Spain has already moved substantially towards a higher wage floor. The minimum wage rose from 41.0% of the median full-time wage in 2018 to 55.3% in 2025, an increase of more than 14 percentage points. France remained above 60%, while Germany and the Netherlands recorded much smaller increases.

Spain’s minimum wage has moved much closer to the median wage

Statutory minimum wage as a percentage of the median full-time wage

Source: OECD, ING Economic Research

The chart above uses the median full-time wage, while PSOE’s proposed legal benchmark refers to the average wage, so the measures are not directly comparable. Both show that further increases would start from a much higher relative level than in 2018. Low-paid employees have recorded the strongest wage growth while employment has continued to rise, but additional increases may be harder for businesses with low productivity or narrow margins.

PSOE would also reduce the standard working week to 37.5 hours without loss of pay and encourage collective bargaining towards 35 hours. Transitional arrangements would support smaller companies, but the combination of higher wages and shorter hours would still raise hourly labour costs. Firms would need to respond through higher productivity, lower margins, higher prices or changes in employment and hours.

The party also wants employers to justify why positions are not offered on a full-time basis and would treat contracts covering more than 80% of a standard schedule as full-time. This targets an important source of low monthly earnings: insufficient paid hours.

Beyond the labour market, PSOE proposes more support for lower-income families through a progressive child benefit, a refundable child tax credit and wider access to childcare and care services. These measures could reach households that receive little from conventional tax allowances, but would also create permanent fiscal costs.

Partido Popular would focus more on disposable income

Partido Popular focuses less on statutory wage targets or shorter working hours and more on tax cuts, incentives for stable employment and support for families.

The party proposes lower personal income tax rates for low and middle-income households, higher personal and family allowances, and an automatic income tax exemption for anyone earning the minimum wage. Tax thresholds would again be adjusted for inflation. Workers and self-employed people aged 18 to 35 would receive a four-year tax reduction, beginning with a full exemption in the first year and declining thereafter.

Tax reductions can increase take-home pay without adding directly to employers’ wage bills. They may therefore carry less immediate employment risk than another large increase in the wage floor. Their reach is weaker at the bottom, however. Workers whose earnings already fall below the income-tax threshold gain little from a conventional tax cut. This includes many people with short working hours.

Partido Popular partly addresses this through refundable family support. Existing deductions would be combined into a monthly payment available even when a household’s tax liability was too low to use the full deduction. The programme also proposes free education from birth to age three, more flexible arrangements for caregivers and a deduction covering 40% of professional care expenses for an elderly dependent relative.

Employers would pay lower unemployment contributions when the stability of their workforce exceeded the average in their sector. New self-employed workers would pay no social security contributions during their first year, with a possible second year for those earning below the minimum wage.

The distributional effect would depend on the balance between conventional tax relief, which offers less to people with little taxable income, and refundable support that can reach poorer households.

Vox would cut taxes and narrow access to benefits

Vox also relies heavily on lower taxation. It proposes a simpler personal income tax system, with rates adjusted for the number of children. Self-employed workers earning below the minimum wage would pay no social security contributions, with contributions rising progressively above that threshold.

Vox would repeal the current government’s labour legislation, which it argues has failed to eliminate insecure employment. The programme promises stable jobs and higher wages, but provides little detail on the rules that would replace the existing framework or how wages would increase.

The party also proposes free education from birth to age three, childcare support and stronger care services. Access would be more restrictive, however. Spanish nationals would receive priority for housing and various social benefits, and the minimum-income scheme would be limited to them.

Foreign nationals are disproportionately represented in the lower wage deciles. These restrictions would therefore reduce support for a group with relatively high exposure to low pay, temporary employment and housing pressure.

The choice concerns instruments, recipients and financing

Gross wages are only one part of household living standards. Tax cuts can raise net earnings but offer little to people with low taxable income, while refundable benefits and public services can reach those households more directly.

The programmes follow a clear left-right divide. PSOE relies on wage regulation, shorter hours, employment protection and public provision. Partido Popular emphasises tax relief, refundable family support and employer incentives. Vox combines broader tax cuts and less labour market regulation with tighter access to benefits.

Ahead of the election on 29 November, most polls point to a parliamentary majority for Partido Popular and Vox. If that produces a government, policy would probably shift towards tax relief, employer incentives and greater labour-market flexibility. The extent of the change would depend on the seat distribution and Vox’s influence.

Spain has shown that strong wage growth at the bottom can coexist with rising employment. Repeating that performance may be harder from today’s higher wage floor, especially when many low-paid employees lack access to sufficient working hours or stable contracts. Higher wage floors and shorter working weeks carry risks for low-productivity employers, while conventional tax cuts often miss the lowest earners. The challenge for the next government will be to raise disposable incomes without weakening employment or creating unsustainable fiscal commitments.

data.title: Two Trades To Watch: DAX, EUR/GBP Forecast - Thursday, Nov. 26
data.description:
DAX rises despite Trump’s tariffs

European shares are rising sharply on Thursday, with banks and tech leading the surge, despite concerns over the Trump administration's plans for new tariffs and the outlook for the AI trade.

A late equity rally in the U.S. last night helped the Nasdaq recover from 4% declines to close just 0.6% lower. This helped fuel a rally in Asia, which then transferred into Europe even after President Trump's latest tariff package.

The proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners use the excuse of combating structural excess industrial capacity. This is just another, different legal route for the same aim of bringing manufacturing back to the U.S., and probably makes as much sense as citing national emergencies.

However, crucially, they would not be on top of the 10% or 12.5% levies imposed in July on a group of 60 trading partners, and they would apply to certain goods.

The hearing on the proposals will not be until January 25, suggesting they may not actually go into effect until the end of Q1, which gives countries more time to prepare.

Meanwhile, on the data front, German consumer confidence gave the markets little reason to cheer. German households remain downbeat amid persistent inflation and sluggish growth, which complicate the outlook. Consumer confidence fell from -30.2 to -30.8, below the expected -29.9.

This doesn't bode well for the Christmas shopping season. It also signals to the ECB that the euro area's largest economy is not doing so well despite a resilient first half of the year. There is a danger that the second half could see stagnating momentum.

For now, policymakers are expected to be able to hike again in December, but the outlook beyond that is less certain.

DAX forecast – technical analysis

After finding support around the 24,500 level, the DAX has recovered higher and is holding above the 200 EMA as well as the 38.2% Fibonacci retracement of the 21,860 low and the 27,000 high. However, the RSI is below 50, suggesting momentum remains weak.

Should this support hold, buyers will need to rise above the rising trendline resistance around 25,500 in order to expose the 50 EMA at 25,700, as well as the 23.6% Fibonacci retracement. Above here, attention turns back to 27,000 and record highs.

Failure to hold above the 200 EMA and the 38.2% Fibonacci level could see the price retest 24,500 (the November low) and 24,450 (the 50% Fibonacci retracement). A break below here turns attention to 23,850, the 61.8% Fibonacci level, ahead of 23,000, the 78.6% Fibonacci level.

EUR/GBP struggles to gain ground as BoE–ECB rate differentials weigh

EUR/GBP is rising very modestly on Thursday but remains within a broader bearish picture.

EUR/GBP had fallen over 2.4% in October, marking its weakest month in over four years. However, those losses have steadied, with the pair so far gaining 0.4% this month as it hovers around 18-month lows.

The pair had come under steep pressure amid increasing hawkish Bank of England expectations. The BoE hiked rates at its November meeting, and the markets are pricing in an 80% probability of a further hike in December. Additionally, the market sees several more rate hikes in the first half of 2027.

This contrasts with the ECB, which has already raised interest rates twice to 2.5%. Whilst the ECB left rates unchanged in October, it signalled a cautious approach to further tightening. The ECB is expected to hike rates again in December, but the path beyond that is less certain, with the potential for one more hike in 2027.

In addition to the BoE–ECB differential, the euro has also been under pressure owing to the French political and fiscal turmoil, although that appears to have calmed for now.

With the pair hovering around levels last seen in April 2025, the latest macro data has failed to provide significant support for the euro after German consumer confidence came in below expectations, around its lowest level in two years.

EUR/GBP forecast – technical analysis

EUR/GBP has been trending lower across 2026 before finding support at 0.8320, a level last seen in March 2025. From here, the price has recovered slightly, pushing above the 20 EMA. However, the broader technical outlook remains bearish, with the price below the 50 and 200 EMAs.

Buyers would need to continue grinding higher towards the 50 EMA at 0.8420 and rise above horizontal resistance at 0.8450 in order to put the price on a firmer footing. Above here, 0.8500 comes into focus, as well as the 200 EMA at 0.8530.

On the downside, immediate support can be seen at the 20 EMA at 0.8360. It would take a break below 0.8320, the 2026 low, to create a lower low and extend the bearish move towards 0.8240, the 2025 low.

data.title: Fallen Angels Take Time To Fly: Decoding Grab Holdings Via Volume Price Analysis
data.description:
An X follower recently asked for my thoughts on two classic “fallen angels”—Grab Holdings (GRAB) and American Battery Technology (ABAT).

As I’ve mentioned in previous posts, if you’ve read my book, The Complete Guide to Volume Price Analysis, you already know how often retail traders are drawn to stocks trading in single digits after suffering a massive post-IPO collapse. Looking at a chart that has fallen from over $17.00 down to $3.00 creates an irresistible urge to hunt for a cheap bargain.

However, the tape’s golden rule is simple: cheap does not automatically mean value. Fallen angels drop fast, but repairing the structural damage can sometimes take years of slow, methodical institutional accumulation.

Because each stock tells a different story, I am covering them separately, starting today with GRAB, which currently shows a stronger institutional and fundamental foundation.

Multi-Timeframe VPA: A Four-Year Lesson in Patience

Looking at the monthly chart of $GRAB, we see a textbook Wyckoff cycle playing out in real time:

  • The Collapse & First Base: After a brutal post-SPAC sell-off, GRAB spent two full years carving out a first-stage accumulation base between $2.50 and $3.85.

  • The Failed Breakout: In November 2024, the stock finally broke through the $3.85 ceiling, posting a high of $5.72, before closing at $5.00, remaining in this region for almost a year and creating a 2nd stage accumulation phase (the pink line on the chart) stalling at $5.72 where overhead supply capped the move for nearly a year creating a 2nd stage accumulation phase.

  • In September 2025, buyers pushed the stock briefly to $6.62 on the highest volume at the time—yet the candle closed with an upper wick.

  • The Slide Back into the Box: October closed on a high-volume doji candle (indecision) also with a high of $6.62. The attempted breakout then collapsed in November around earnings. By March 2026, GRAB had slid straight back into its old $2.50-$3.85 accumulation box, spending five months grinding against the $3.85 ceiling (now reinforced by the downward-sloping 50-month moving average sitting around $4.77).

The VPA Reality: Absorption at the $2.50 Floor

However, just when the chart looked broken this autumn, the volume bars revealed a dramatic shift in institutional behaviour.

As the price drifted back toward the $2.50 macro floor, $GRAB printed the highest monthly volume bars in its corporate history: a staggering 1.58 billion shares in September 2026, followed by 1.39 billion shares in October 2026 and so far this month $1.69 billion shares.

In VPA terms, this is an unmistakable Effort vs. Result anomaly. Massive volume on a compressed down candle confirms absorption. While retail traders were capitulating on the failed breakout, large institutional buyers stepped in to absorb every available share.

By cross-referencing these huge volumes with off-exchange institutional activity, we can see how that big money is actively defending this zone.

During the November 18th trading session—as $GRAB closed near the $3.13/14 price points —institutional block activity surged sharply, clustering tightly around the $3.14 mark:

  • A massive off-exchange block of 20.0 million shares (worth $62.8 million) crossed the tape at exactly $3.14.

  • This was backed up at the market close by a 3.6 million share Closing Auction block ($11.3 million) at $3.14, alongside multi-million-dollar institutional blocks layering earlier in the afternoon at $3.17 (7.93M) and $3.18 (3.38M, $1.46M, and $1.20M).

When institutions execute $60M+ block trades at a single decimal tick off-exchange, they are establishing a concrete institutional price floor.

November will now close on the highest volume ever for GRAB – $1.7 billion at time of writing and we will have to wait until next week to determine the candle.

  • Daily Weakness vs. Weekly Containment: While the recent slide lower looks discouraging, the weekly chart shows price action is still within the November Nov 2nd volatility candle, whose low sits at $2.75. Until $2.74 breaks on heavy volume, the market is still consolidating inside an institutional range.

C-Suite Activity

CEO Anthony Tan purchased $29.9 million of stock at $2.89 in late September, backed by $GRAB repurchasing $400 million of its own shares this autumn. Combined with Q3 profitability across all core segments and a $1 billion AI partnership with SoftBank, the fundamental floor is also firming up.

The Options Shift & Technical Consensus

Since I first began my analysis of $GRAB, the derivatives landscape has undergone a dramatic bullish shift. After weeks of heavy defensive hedging, the Put/Call ratio has fallen from a very bearish 2.51 to a bullish 0.22, coinciding with “Strong Buy” consensus signals.

Even so, we must respect the levels on the options ladder:

  • Gamma Flip Level: $3.15

  • Call Wall (Immediate Ceiling): $3.00

  • Put Wall (Macro Floor): $2.50

Trading near $2.84 (at the time of writing), $GRAB remains in a Negative Gamma regime (below $3.15), meaning dealer hedging can still amplify short-term swings, while the $3.00 Call Wall acts as immediate overhead resistance. Meanwhile, a modest 6.26% short float indicates any recovery will be driven by steady accumulation rather than a violent short squeeze.

The Technical Verdict

GRAB remains locked inside its $2.50 to $3.85 multi-year range, but the combination of historic monthly absorption, a 0.22 Put/Call ratio, improved fundamentals, coupled with ‘Strong Buy’ recommendations suggests the bottoming process is maturing.

  • The Line in the Sand ($2.74): Watch the $2.74 weekly volatility candle low. Holding above this level—backed by the $2.81 closing blocks—keeps the weekly containment intact.

  • Breakout Confirmation: Reclaiming the $3.00 Call Wall and punching above the $3.15 Gamma Flip shifts dealers back into stabilising Positive Gamma, opening a clean runway back toward the $3.85 range ceiling.

data.title: Royal Bank Of Canada Forecast Ahead Of Earnings: Will It Rebound Or Fall?
data.description:
Royal Bank of Canada (RY) stock has dropped into a correction, moving from a record high of $306 in July to $269 today. This retreat has coincided with the ongoing weakness of Canadian and US banks. Focus now shifts to its earnings, which will come out on December 3.

RBC Bank is falling as global banks drop

Royal Bank of Canada, the biggest bank in Canada, is a top player that offers diverse services, including personal banking, commercial banking, wealth management, insurance, and capital markets. It has the biggest market share in the country, which helps it generate over $66 billion a year.

RBC stock has dropped recently because of the ongoing weakness in the banking industry. A closer look at most banks stocks shows that many of them have pulled back in the past few months. 

The most recent results showed that RBC’s business did well in the second quarter, with its revenue rising by 11% to $18.3 billion. The closely-watched net income rose to $6 billion, while the return on equity rose to 17.9%.

READ MORE: Royal Bank of Canada stock double-tops ahead of Q1 earnings

Most of its businesses did well during the quarter. For example, its wealth management division grew by 32% to $1.44 billion, helped by its higher fee-based assets. Its commercial banking revenue rose by 12% to $936 million, while its capital markets segment made $1.54 billion, up by 16% from a year earlier. 

These segments helped to offset the decline in its insurance and personal computing business. 

RBC to publish earnings next week

Therefore, looking ahead, the upcoming earnings report is expected to show that its business continued growing, driven by its wealth management division. 

The challenge, however, is that its capital markets business likely remained under pressure in the fourth fiscal quarter. This business has been relatively weak because of the rising interest rates. Indeed, a report by the London Stock Exchange showed that global deal value dropped by 41% in the third quarter to $993 billion. 

Most companies also published slower investment banking revenue. Morgan Stanley’s investment banking revenue rose by 2% to $2.16 billion, while Citigroup’s, JPMorgan, and Goldman Sachs grew by 9%, 15%, and 21%, respectively. 

Yahoo Finance data shows that analysts expect the upcoming earnings to show that its revenue rose by 7.37% to $18.48 billion. The earnings per share is expected to move to $4.15 from $3.85 in the same period last year. Investors will focus on its net income margin and its wealth management and investment banking business. Also, markets will react to its costs, which have been rising recently. Its non-interest expense rose by 6% in the third quarter.

Analysts have a muted outlook for the company. Scotiabank reiterated its outperform rating, while Barclays maintained its overweight position. TD Securities also maintained a buy rating, while Raymond James downgraded its rating from outperform to market outperform. The average target among analysts on its US shares is $227, up by 20% from the current level. 

RBC stock price technical analysis

RBC stock chart | Source: TradingView

The daily chart shows that the Royal Bank of Canada share price has been under pressure in the past few months. It dropped from $306 in June to the current $268. 

The stock has now settled along the 23.6% Fibonacci Retracement level, which also coincides with the lowest level on October 8. It has dropped below the 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA) and the Supertrend indicator.

The stock has already invalidated the double-bottom pattern at $268. Therefore, there is a risk that it continues falling, potentially to the 61.8% Fibonacci Retracement level at $247, which is about 8.2% below the current level.

data.title: FX Daily: Korean Won Stands Out In A Harsh EM Environment
data.description:
It looks like the sell-off in risk assets has run its course for now, with investors starting to find value in equities, commodities and some FX pairs. How long this calm lasts is unknown, since it looks like the Fed will have to push ahead with tightening. To withstand dollar strength, currencies will need a good story. The Korean won has one.

The Korean won remains one of our preferred currencies for 2027.

USD: Defining boundaries

In another wild ride for risk assets yesterday, it seems that investors are starting to carve out some boundaries. Levels below 7000 in the S&P 500, below $12,000/MT in copper and above 104.50 in the DXY all seem to be sufficient re-pricing for the time being. Whether it was the sharp fall in short-dated US rates yesterday that helped risk assets – on views that the Fed would have to soften its tightening stance – remains to be seen. But at one point, two-year US swap rates were 12bp lower on the day. They have since retraced a large chunk of that drop.

The problem in calling a more durable recovery in risk assets from here is that the Fed looks certain to tighten in December and remain hawkish. Third quarter growth came in at more than 4% quarter-on-quarter annualised, the labour market seems to be picking up and inflation is re-accelerating from levels well above target. As many commentators have said, the bar for the Fed to come and save risk assets with a softer monetary policy stance is high.

As such, there seems to be no reason to expect a much weaker dollar in the near term. However, some stability in risk assets can allow good stories to come through, such as in Korea (see below) and perhaps Brazil too, if President Lula opts for a market-friendly finance minister in the form of Bradesco’s chairman.

With the US out for Thanksgiving today, expect very quiet markets, with DXY probably drifting at the bottom of a 103.50-104.50 range.

EUR: Consolidation kicks in

Let's start with the positives. EUR/USD has held support at 1.0880 this week and a close tomorrow around the current level (1.0975) would suggest the first week of reversal since dollar strength drove this 7% EUR/USD drop since late August. December normally sees a weaker dollar and this week's EUR/USD drop substantially overshot short-term rate differentials. Lower energy prices this month have also improved the eurozone's terms of trade, which the euro is yet to adjust to.

The problem is that the central drivers of dollar strength – a strong US economy, inflation above target and a hawkish Fed – remain fully intact. Looking at US real rates, the drop in inflation expectations this week has outpaced the drop in nominal rates and the two-year real swap rate remains at 2.40%, matching the highs from 2023. This, we think, is central to the sell-off in precious metals and bitcoin.

For today, the focus will be on the release of the ECB minutes from the October meeting and potentially an announcement on the new leadership team at the central bank.

Expect EUR/USD to trade in a tight range not far from 1.0975 today, and it is not clear what the catalysts will be for a break back above 1.10 next week.

CEE: Pushing the limits

Yesterday’s continuation of the global risk-off sentiment and de-risking confirmed our bearish bias for the region, with the CZK outperforming its peers. EUR/PLN and EUR/HUF tested new highs yesterday. With the US market closed or subdued for the next two days, the market might see some stabilisation in the region following a difficult few days.

Nevertheless, the bearish arguments remain; in our view, EUR/PLN, in particular, has further upside potential. Despite the rally in rates over the last few days, the market is still pricing in roughly 10bp of easing for the National Bank of Poland's December meeting. We, however, do not expect the first rate hikes until the first quarter of 2027. November inflation data, out on Monday, could prove decisive. If our expectations are confirmed, the unwinding of rate-hike expectations should open up further upside for EUR/PLN above 4.500.

On the other hand, EUR/HUF tested the 374 level again yesterday, which appears to be a ceiling. We have seen some hawkish comments from the National Bank of Hungary this week, suggesting that the central bank is not pleased with recent FX moves. We therefore believe that 374 could serve as a cap for now, and the NBH might potentially introduce further measures to keep the exchange rate under control.

Similarly, as we noted here yesterday regarding EUR/CZK, the 24.450 level has proven to be a cap for now. The pair is benefiting from a hawkish central bank, the only one to have raised rates since the onset of the US-Iran conflict.

KRW: Bank of Korea hikes, story looks good

In hiking rates to 3.25% today, the Bank of Korea gave a notably upbeat assessment of the Korean economy. Its forecasts assume that strong semiconductor demand will extend into 2027, prompting it to raise its GDP growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 to 3.9% and 4.1%, respectively, from 3.3% and 2.9%.

Exports and investment are driving those gains, and it expects weakish domestic consumption to slowly catch up too. Even though there was a 5-2 vote for the 25bp rate hike today, the expectation is that another 25bp rate hike is expected next year, which would see the policy rate matching the 23/24 cycle high of 3.50%.

From an FX perspective, it notes that it needs to match expected rate hikes from the Fed to avoid a weaker won adding to the inflation problem. (This stands in stark contrast to Banxico.) But more importantly, it has revised up its forecast for Korea's current account surplus to $500bn this year and $540bn next year. It's hard to think that Korea's prior record current account surplus was $123bn in 2025. Strong domestic growth rates mean that these overseas earnings can come home and that won strength will be welcomed.

The Korean won was one of our preferred currencies in our 2027 FX Outlook, and our end-2027 USD/KRW target of 1275 feels a little conservative.

data.title: German Consumers Still Don’t Share Companies’ Optimism
data.description:
While leading business sentiment indicators like the Ifo index and the PMI point to a continuation of the cyclical rebound of the German economy, consumers' wallets remain closed.

German consumers still aren’t buying the resilience story business sentiment indicators are telling. According to the latest GfK consumer confidence indicator, consumer sentiment has improved only marginally and remains well below its September level. Likely reflecting labour market uncertainty and the impact of higher prices, consumers’ propensity to save remains high, while their appetite to spend remains close to historic lows. More concerning for the ECB, price expectations have risen further.

Since the 2022 energy shock, German consumer confidence has sat deeply in negative territory. Against this background, stagnating and sometimes even positive private consumption has been a surprise. This year, however, private consumption is back as a drag on growth. The worsening labour market, with dropping employment and increasing unemployment, as well as weakening real wages combined with job insecurity and the energy price shock, has kept German wallets closed.

Looking ahead, it is hard to see how the German consumer could suddenly transform from a drag into a growth driver. The macro backdrop for consumers is hardly going to change. Precautionary savings rather than a spending spree is the most likely scenario for 2027.

All in all, this morning’s disappointing consumer confidence puts the latest improvements in other leading indicators, like the Ifo index and PMIs, into perspective. If anything, the current cyclical rebound has clearly not reached consumers, and with high energy prices, labour market uncertainty and higher interest rates, it is doubtful that it actually will.

data.title: These 3 Retail Stocks Are Best Positioned To Benefit From Thanksgiving In 2026
data.description:
The Thanksgiving shopping rush looks a little smaller this year.

The National Retail Federation estimates 182.7 million consumers plan to shop between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, down from 186.9 million last year.

Black Friday alone is expected to draw 126 million shoppers.

With more consumers starting early, the retailers best positioned to benefit are the ones giving shoppers several reasons to spend across the weekend.

Walmart can turn a grocery trip into a gift purchase, Target is using exclusives to bring people into stores, and Amazon (AMZN) is putting deals inside a football broadcast.

Walmart can turn a $35 dinner into a bigger shopping basket

Walmart (WMT) advertised a 26-item Thanksgiving meal basket for $35 that serves 10. At $3.5 a person, the offer gives households a concrete reason to choose it for one of November’s biggest grocery trips.

The payoff can come from what shoppers add to the order, from roasting pans and extra desserts to toys they were already planning to buy.

Walmart’s main Black Friday sale went online Nov. 23, overlapping with the final days of Thanksgiving prep.

In-store deals begin Friday morning. That timing matters because Walmart’s US e-commerce sales rose 23% in its latest quarter.

A customer who orders groceries online can browse holiday deals in the same place, giving Walmart another chance to win the gift purchase before that shopper opens a rival’s app.

Target gives Black Friday shoppers a reason to show up

Target (TGT) has $30 Thanksgiving meal for six but the bigger opportunity comes Friday morning. The first 100 eligible shoppers at each store get a gift card, with one card per location worth $1,000.

Target is also rolling out exclusive Pokémon and Topps trading-card products. A giveaway can get people through the door. An exclusive gives them something to buy that they can’t easily price-check at a rival.

Target enters the weekend with store comparable sales up 4.6% in its latest quarter.

The question for investors is how much of that traffic turns into a fuller cart. A shopper who comes for a collectible and leaves with holiday décor, wrapping paper or another gift makes the promotion more valuable than the giveaway alone would suggest.

Amazon brings the sale to the football audience

Amazon’s (AMZN) holiday sale runs through Nov. 30, with two rounds of featured deals on both Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Its most distinctive sales pitch comes during Friday’s Pittsburgh Steelers–Denver Broncos game on Prime Video.

Viewers can use their remote or the Amazon Shopping app to see featured deals and buy merchandise during the broadcast, giving Amazon a chance to reach people who tuned in for football and may never have planned to browse a sale.

That extra attention has value beyond the items Amazon sells directly. Independent merchants can pay Amazon for services such as fulfillment, and brands can pay for ad placements.

For investors, that means a busy shopping weekend can generate revenue for Amazon even when another merchant makes the sale.

data.title: Micron And SanDisk Stocks Among The Cheapest In Tech: Should You Buy?
data.description:
Micron Technology (MU) and SanDisk (SNDK) have emerged among the most attractively valued stocks in the information technology sector, according to a recent valuation screen.

However, their low earnings multiples are raising questions about whether investors are overlooking an opportunity or anticipating a downturn in the memory industry.

The two companies have been major beneficiaries of rising demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure, as hyperscalers and technology companies invest heavily in data centres, high-bandwidth memory and storage capacity.

Yet their shares have come under pressure amid a broader sell-off in semiconductor stocks, driven by concerns that AI spending may be running ahead of the revenue and profits it can ultimately generate.

Investors are also weighing the possibility of tighter political and regulatory scrutiny of data centre construction, alongside expectations of a potential Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

Micron has fallen over 33% in the last month, while SanDisk is down over 53%.

Micron and SanDisk rank among the cheapest technology stocks

As the third-quarter earnings season draws to a close, investors are reassessing valuations across the technology sector.

Companies are experiencing different growth trajectories and margin pressures despite continued demand for AI infrastructure, semiconductors, and enterprise technology.

According to Seeking Alpha's Quant Ratings, 20 information technology stocks have attractive relative valuations.

Eight companies received an A+ Valuation Grade, the highest possible rating.

They include Arrow Electronics (ARW), Diodes (DIOD), DXC Technology (DXC), Fastly (FSLY), Micron, MaxLinear (MXL), Super Micro Computer (SMCI), and SanDisk.

The valuation discount for the two memory companies is particularly striking.

According to GuruFocus data as of November 26, SanDisk traded at 4.7 times trailing earnings, while Micron traded at 8.1 times.

Both were substantially below the sector peer median of 29.8 times.

Their forward price-to-earnings ratios were even lower, at 2.58 for SanDisk and 3.4 for Micron.

The stocks were also trading well below their respective 52-week highs, with SanDisk down 75% and Micron down 52%.

However, low multiples do not necessarily indicate that a stock is undervalued.

Memory prices are highly sensitive to changes in supply and demand, and exceptionally strong earnings can quickly deteriorate when the industry enters a weaker phase.

Why low P/E ratios may be a warning for memory stocks

The cyclical nature of the memory business is one reason investors remain cautious despite the apparent valuation opportunity.

Brendan Burke, research director for semiconductors, supply chain and emerging technology at the Futurum Group, described low price-to-earnings ratios for memory companies as a "warning label, not a bargain sign."

"Investors have learned over decades to sell memory stocks at peak earnings, because the earnings side of that ratio has historically collapsed when the cycle turns," he said in a MarketWatch report.

"A multiple in the low single digits tells you the market is pricing today's profits as a peak," he added.

However, Burke acknowledged that the current AI investment cycle may differ from previous memory booms.

The historical precedent "ignores that AI has changed the shape of this cycle."

Some types of memory, including high-bandwidth memory and solid-state-drive storage, are tied to what he called "mission-critical data-center buildouts", rather than demand for memory used in personal computers and handsets.

That distinction could make earnings "more durable than these multiples imply," Burke said.

William Blair analyst Sebastien Naji told MarketWatch that there was a limit to the usefulness of low P/E ratios as a "valuation support metric."

CreditSights analyst Andy Li also cautioned that memory stocks experience "extreme volatility in pricing", which can produce boom-and-bust cycles.

If investors continue to treat the sector as cyclical, a "dramatic price decline may well be in the cards," he said. "The price action reflects that fear."

Li explained that cyclical stocks often trade at "very low" price-to-earnings multiples near market peaks because their estimated earnings for the next 12 months are "most inflated".

They tend to bottom at relatively high multiples as earnings estimates contract.

He also pointed to the monthly options expiry on Friday as a possible technical factor influencing the stocks.

Strong AI demand faces questions over future supply

Recent financial results underline the strength of demand for memory and storage products.

Micron reported fiscal fourth-quarter 2026 revenue of $54.23 billion, compared with $11.32 billion a year earlier.

The company forecast revenue of $61.5 billion for the following quarter.

SanDisk reported $11 billion in fiscal first-quarter 2027 revenue and expects sales of between $12.2 billion and $12.6 billion in the next quarter.

The challenge for investors is determining whether these growth rates and margins can be sustained as memory producers expand capacity and more supply enters the market.

That concern has prompted some brokerages to reassess their outlook for Micron.

BNP Paribas downgraded the company to Neutral from Outperform earlier this week and cut its price target to $775 from $1,700.

The brokerage cited potential delays to data centre capacity expansion and reductions in memory content.

"Yes, Micron's shares have fallen 42% from its peak in June, but growing risks to hyperscaler capacity plans in 2028 further threaten S/D fundamentals while HBM content is being reduced in Vera Rubin Ultra, PC and mobile units will decline in ’26 and ’27, and incremental wafer capacity comes online," said BNP analyst Karl Ackerman in a Tuesday note.

"We think the downside risk to an oversupply scenario is mounting with growing risks of data center permit delays to 2028 data center capacity, content reductions in AI servers, PC, and mobile, and accelerated memory capacity by memory producers," he added.

"We think DRAM and NAND supply-demand can approach parity starting in mid-2027 and result in ASP declines, earlier than our prior view of mid-2028."

BNP now expects memory and storage costs associated with AI spending to peak at 40% in 2027 before declining to 27% by calendar year 2030.

UBS (UBS) has also scaled back its bullish outlook.

On November 25, analyst Timothy Arcuri cut his price target on Micron to $1,100 from $1,625, while retaining a Buy rating.

The contrasting signals leave investors weighing two competing possibilities: AI demand could sustain a longer and stronger memory cycle than historical patterns suggest, or current earnings could represent a cyclical peak.

For Micron and SanDisk, the sustainability of pricing and margins may ultimately matter more than how inexpensive their shares appear on conventional valuation measures.

data.title: Minutes Of ECB’s October Meeting Confirm Tightening Bias
data.description:
The minutes of the ECB's October meeting confirm a clear tightening bias and suggest a rate hike at the December meeting is almost a done deal.

The just-released minutes of the ECB’s October meeting confirmed the central bank's current tightening bias. Given that many ECB members had already been in favour of a rate hike at the October meeting, a December hike looks almost like a done deal. On a slightly different note, the minutes also shed new light on the ECB’s internal arithmetic: a large number of members can still fall short of a majority.

Here are the most important passages from the minutes:

Waiting until December to get a better picture of the longer-term inflation forecast. "The December projections, which would extend the forecast horizon to include 2029, would provide an updated integrated assessment of how the energy shock, AI-related dynamics, the shift in financing conditions and all other relevant developments were shaping the inflation outlook and the surrounding risks."

Concerns about the growth outlook. "Looking ahead, members generally agreed that tightening financial conditions and the renewed spike in energy prices would have a negative effect on growth, although its magnitude remained to be seen. The decline in demand for loans suggested a stronger adverse effect on activity than had been seen so far, although some of the effect from higher rates on private investment spending, housing and consumption might be attenuated by the weaker exchange rate."

Inflation remains primarily an energy price shock (for now). "Members concurred with the assessment presented by Philip Lane in his introduction, noting that, on the one hand, energy prices had increased beyond the baseline path foreseen in the September ECB staff projections, which was likely to raise inflation further in the near term and keep headline inflation well above target over the coming year. On the other hand, underlying inflation had remained broadly stable in recent months and wage growth data had moderated further."

Some concerns about sticky inflation. "Regarding the near-term outlook, on the one hand, it was clear that inflation would be higher for longer than previously expected. On the other hand, the latest data for inflation in the HICP excluding energy and food suggested a slightly better outlook than previously expected, but allowing for pass-through from higher energy prices would suggest a higher core inflation trajectory at or above the level seen in the adverse scenario. It was suggested that perhaps underlying inflation could become sticky at around 2.5% rather than receding."

Not giving up on those indirect effects. "Regarding the direct, indirect and second-round effects from higher energy prices, thus far it was mostly direct effects that were materialising. Indirect effects had overall remained limited, as expected, and so far there were no material signs of second-round effects. However, the fact that energy prices had risen even higher and for longer, together with the signals from input prices and selling price expectations, suggested that indirect effects would become stronger over time and some second-round effects would eventually materialise, as already anticipated to a degree in the September projections."

A large number is not a majority. "A large number of members noted that, as the incoming data since the September Governing Council meeting had confirmed the case for further policy tightening, they could have supported raising interest rates at the current meeting. These members stressed that a further rate hike was warranted in light of the deteriorating inflation outlook, while acknowledging elevated uncertainty, the impact of higher yields on financial conditions and the limited evidence so far of second-round effects."

All in all, a clear confirmation of the ECB's tightening bias, based on the assumption that high energy prices will eventually still translate into broader inflationary pressure; a development that is not yet the case.

Preparing for a December hike

Today's minutes confirmed ECB President Christine Lagarde’s message at the October press conference. The fact that several ECB members openly advocated a rate hike, even if they fell short of a majority, sends a clear signal. If the macro backdrop at the upcoming December meeting (on 18 December) is similar to the one in October, a rate hike is a done deal. The only limitations to this ‘done deal’ scenario we have heard since then, at least from the doves, are that oil prices and financing conditions could move quickly, potentially in a direction making another hike obsolete.

Looking at these external circumstances, oil prices have indeed fallen significantly since the ECB’s October meeting but are not much lower than when the September staff projections were conducted. As regards financing conditions, the drop in bond yields since September will bring little respite for ECB doves. Last but not least, the latest weakening of the euro will probably enter the ECB’s radar screen again these days. Since the September projections, the nominal effective exchange rate has lost some 3%. Adding all these elements together, there will be very little reason to give the ‘all clear’ on inflation.

Let’s stick with the next round of ECB staff projections for a minute. Next to changes in the so-called technical assumptions, the most interesting elements of the forecasts will be the forecasts for wage growth and core inflation. Up to now, the ECB seems to stick to the traditional approach that higher energy prices will eventually translate into higher core inflation and wage growth. Even if there haven’t been any indications of such developments so far.

When it comes to wage growth forecasts, in particular, the ECB has been much more optimistic than, for example, the Survey of Professional Forecasters. In our view, final demand remains under too much stress from higher energy prices and labour market insecurity to eventually see a significant increase in core inflation. Instead, corporate profit margin squeezing will be the new game in town. So far, the ECB has had a different view. Let’s see whether this could change at the December meeting.

Today's minutes as well as recent official comments confirm our view that the ECB will hike again by 25bp at the December meeting. Beyond the December meeting, however, the path for monetary policy is less obvious. In fact, it will depend on whether the still-not-visible impact of higher energy prices on the rest of the economy eventually materialises. We are less convinced than the ECB and therefore think that additional rate hikes in 2027 would do more harm than good.

data.title: When A Stock Falls, Is The Business Really In Trouble?
data.description:
When a stock falls, has the business weakened or has the price come back in line with earnings? Chuck Carnevale uses FAST Graphs to show how earnings growth, cash flow, and the price you pay can shape long-term returns.

When a Stock Falls, Is the Business Really in Trouble?

A falling stock price tells you what investors are willing to pay today. To understand what the business is worth, look at what it earns, how much cash it generates, and what you can reasonably expect it to earn in the future.

In this FAST Graphs video, Chuck Carnevale demonstrates a simple way to start. He takes the stock price off the chart and looks at how the business performed on its own. Then he puts the price back on the chart to see where it tracked earnings and where it pulled away. It’s a practical application of a theme from All Investing Is Value Investing, the book Chuck co-authored with Professor Nathan Mauck.

A strong business can still be an expensive stock

Oracle (ORCL) and Amgen (AMGN) both grew earnings through difficult economic periods. Yet the returns Chuck shows vary widely depending on what an investor paid. In one Amgen example, buying at a lower valuation produced a higher annualized return than buying at a premium during a period of faster earnings growth. The starting price mattered enough to outweigh the difference in growth.

Alphabet (GOOGL) illustrates another point. Change the time frame on a FAST Graphs chart and the historical earnings growth rate can change with it. That can shift the valuation reference. Comparing several periods helps you see whether a particular growth rate reflects a sustained record or an unusually strong stretch.

Do the numbers support the business story?

Copart (CPRT) offers a concrete example of a competitive advantage. Its salvage yards and insurer relationships bring vehicles to auction, and a global network of buyers makes those auctions more valuable to insurers. Each side helps attract the other. That explains why the business has been hard to replicate. The valuation question is how much to pay for that advantage if future earnings grow more slowly than they did in the past.

Chuck asks a similar question about NVIDIA (NVDA). Using Ask Charles, he looks at how NVIDIA’s CUDA software ecosystem supports its competitive position and what the company’s balance sheet and cash generation say about the business. The valuation still depends on whether NVIDIA can deliver the earnings growth investors expect.

What does it take to recover from a 50% loss?

If a $100 investment falls to $50, it takes a 100% gain to get back to $100. Even a 30% rally would bring it only to $65. That’s why the size of a rebound tells you so little on its own. The price you paid and the earnings the business can deliver still matter.

Watch the full video to see how Chuck uses FAST Graphs to compare earnings and stock prices, weigh growth expectations, and look for a margin of safety.

data.title: Fed Rate-Hike Bets Deliver Fresh Blow To Your Holiday Budget
data.description:
American households are getting squeezed from all sides this holiday season as stubborn inflation and a stronger-than-expected U.S. economy collide with a fresh wave of proposed tariffs.

For America’s consumers and borrowers, their money worries are no longer just a single interest-rate hike in December but perhaps a relentless tightening cycle that could push the Federal Reserve to keep raising the benchmark federal funds rate through January, March, and possibly beyond before rate cuts could resume in 2028.

“Additional tariffs complicate the inflation situation along with the lingering ways in which supply chains have been roiled due to the AI buildout, KPMG Chief Economist and Managing Director Diane Swonk said in a blog post. “The Fed is in a tough spot in December, weighing another rate hike but concerned about the speed with which a larger market correction could ripple through the economy.”  

Fresh economic PCE readings of hot, sticky, and broadening inflation in October and revised, sharply higher third-quarter GDP at 4.3% — the fastest pace since late 2023 — released Nov. 25 give central bankers ample reasons to lean hawkish with a 25-basis-point rate hike at the Federal Open Market Committee Dec. 8-9.

Minutes after those headlines crossed, the Trump administration unveiled proposed new tariffs targeting 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan, and the European Union, to counter what the administration calls foreign “excess industrial capacity.”

Truist Advisory Services Head of U.S. Economics Mike Skordeles said the year-over-year increase of headline and core PCE and the revised GDP report further confirm “for us that the Fed will deliver a quarter-point hike in December.’’ 

Skordeles said in an exclusive email to TheStreet that the proposed tariffs won’t be enacted until January at the earliest and won’t affect specific industries with national security-related levies, such as steel, aluminum and automobiles.

“The combination of the factors should limit the near-term implications, especially for most consumers,” Skordeles said. 

Persistent inflation puts Fed rate hikes in focus

The FOMC held rates steady in October at 3.75-4.0% after a 25-basis-point hike in September, amid sticky inflation from tariffs, the Iran War energy shock, and the AI demand-supply dynamic. It was the Fed’s first rate move of the year.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh vowed before and after taking over the role in May that the price stability side of its dual mandate is the independent central bank’s top commitment now that the labor market has stabilized from its 2025 softness.

Four Fed governors — Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, Michael Barr, Lisa Cook and Christopher Waller — and several regional bank presidents recently signaled decidedly hawkish tones, expressing that further policy tightening was necessary to bring inflation back to its 2% target, which it has missed for nearly six years. 

The Fed made three 25-basis-point cuts at its last three meetings of 2025 due to concerns about the labor market side of its mandate. Those insurance cuts need to be reversed as inflation data shows higher prices not only in energy costs but broadening into other sectors including services, the Fed’s hawks say.

So do some Fed watchers. Wall Street banks, including giants J.P. Morgan, Bank of America and Deutsche Bank, are also calling for a 25-basis-point hike in December plus additional 25-basis-point increases in January and March.

TheStreet

Traders price in Fed rate hikes into 2027  

According to the CME Group FedWatch Tool, following the latest inflation readings, futures traders see roughly a 97% to 98% probability of a 25-point-rate hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.

But it probably won’t be a “one-and-done” deal.

CME FedWatch probabilities for the January FOMC meeting point to a strong chance of additional tightening, including a roughly 40.7% probability of another 25-basis-point hike and a 58.4% chance of a cumulative 50-basis-point increase. Markets also price in an additional rate increase in March if policymakers are unable to cool demand.

President Donald Trump and his allies have repeatedly called for lower interest rates of 1% or less for years, with the president blasting the Fed’s most recent actions as political retribution.

Trump has said the lower rates will help the depressed U.S. housing market plus reduce the interest the government pays on its $40.71 trillion debt.  

New tariffs aim to boost, balance American trade

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer’s office unveiled the proposals following an eight-month investigation into foreign industrial overcapacity and set the maximum potential tariff rates of 20% to 40%.

Separately, the administration proposed a new 10% tariff on finished commercial aircraft from Brazil and higher duties on over-quota Brazilian sugar after talks with the South American nation stalled.

The new tariff push, while not viewed as sweeping as April’s Liberation Day announcement, lands just three weeks after midterm elections reflected voter frustration over higher costs of living and skepticism about Wall Street, where volatility has been fueled by AI and other tech jitters. 

Dean Lyulkin, the CEO of Cardiff, a San Diego-based small business lender, said the Trump administration’s proposed tariffs fall mainly on Vietnam and Southeast Asia, and mostly on furniture, clothing, and other consumer goods.

“Even there, the additional tariff applies to the wholesale import value, not the retail price, and amounts to just 5% to 10% more,’’ Lyulkin said in an exclusive email to TheStreet.

Critics warn that new import levies amount to a tax on consumers and risk triggering another round of price increases that could force the Fed to keep interest rates higher for longer.

“There is zero reason for anyone, including investors and small business owners, to panic,’’ Lyulkin said. “If this headline is used to explain the market correction happening now, or to suggest it adds new risks to the U.S. economy, that line of thinking can be quickly dismissed as nonsense.”

Fed struggles to lower inflation to 2% target

For households carrying credit-card balances, private student loans or adjustable-rate debt, each 25-basis-point hike adds up—and analysts warn that sustained rate hikes could lift Treasury yields and keep borrowing costs elevated well into mid-2027.

“The challenge for the Fed is that we need to see 0.2% or less monthly core PCE gains consistently to return inflation to its 2% target,’’ Swonk said, describing the last nearly six years of price pressures as “the longest and most corrosive bout of inflation since the 1970s.”

“A fall in pump prices and more promotions among retailers could get us there in November – but it may not stay there,’’ Swonk said.

data.title: A Textbook Sequence Of Selling And Buying
data.description:
A selling cluster, a buying thrust and a retest: what the market internals say, and what followed in the past

Last week's heavy selling came in a cluster: three days in six sessions with more than 80% of the S&P 500's dollar volume in falling stocks, the third on November 19. On Monday came the thrust: 90% of the dollar volume in rising stocks and the futures up 4.6% in a day. Tuesday gave a little back. Wednesday opened with a flush that took the S&P 500 down 3.2% and the Nasdaq 100 down 4.8% from Tuesday's close, and then the market spent the rest of the day buying it back.

The S&P 500 still finished lower, by 0.25% at 7,182.78. That number hides the more important part of the day: most stocks closed higher, many of them well higher.

What happened under the surface

· Most stocks rose. 371 of the S&P 500's 502 stocks closed up (74%). 89% closed above their opening price, and 86% closed in the top half of the day's range.

· The average stock beat the index. The equal-weight S&P 500 (RSP) gained 0.83% while the cap-weighted index (SPY) lost 0.29%. Midcaps (MDY) rose 1.16%, the Russell 2000 (IWM) 0.65% and the NYSE Composite 0.61%.

· The losses sat in the giants. The Nasdaq 100 lost 0.65% after a 4.8% intraday drop, and 59% of the S&P 500's dollar volume still went into falling stocks: the money traded in the largest names, and they fell. The red close of the index came from a handful of its heaviest weights, not from the market as a whole.

· The flush was bought hard. The S&P 500 closed at 93% of the day's range, 3.1% above its low. The futures traded down to 6,982.5, a few points under Monday's thrust-day low of 6,992, and closed near 7,206. The cash index traded 2.5% under Monday's low of 7,153 and closed back above it.

Strong breadth under a red index: what followed in the past

A day when the S&P 500 falls while the equal-weight version beats it by a full point is not common. Since 2003 it happened 23 times, and both Tuesday and Wednesday of this week qualified.

 Three things stand out:

· The payoff came over months, not weeks. Three months later SPY was higher in 19 of 20 cases, by 6.8% on average, more than twice an ordinary three months. The next month was no better than average.

· It did not prevent more selling first. The two cases earlier this fall, October 8 and October 22, were followed by drops of 5.0% and 9.7% within a month. They came at the start of this decline. Broad strength under a weak index says the selling is narrow; it doesn't say it is over.

· The reversal alone is not the signal. Days when SPY fell 2.5% or more intraday and closed near its high happened 18 times, and a month later SPY was lower on average (−2.8%, up only 47% of the time): those days come in turbulent markets. What made Wednesday different is the breadth. Only one other day combined a 2% intraday flush, a close near the high and equal weight beating SPY by a point: January 27, 2025, the day the DeepSeek news hit the AI stocks. SPY was 7.8% lower three months later, after the April tariff drop. One case is a caution, not a pattern.

How it fits the bigger picture

· The sequence is the textbook one. A selling cluster, then a thrust, then a retest. Since 2000 a buying thrust after a selling cluster has been followed by a dip back to the thrust day's low more often than not. In the 24 past cases where that low was tested and the close held above it, SPY was up 2.0% a month later (71% of the time) and 2.9% after three months. When the closes stayed above the thrust day's low for the next two weeks (10 of the 24), the month averaged +3.7%.

· Fear is extreme. The CIT Balance of Power fear and greed gauge closed at 17, deep in extreme fear, and the CBOE put/call ratio's 10-day average sits in the top tenth of the past year. Since 2008, readings like this were followed by an average month of +2.2% for the S&P 500 (up 73% of the time, against +0.9% for all days), but also by a 10% drop within three months 23% of the time, against 16% normally. Fear marks the best months and the worst ones.

· The broad market has been leading for weeks. Equal weight has beaten the cap-weighted S&P 500 by 5.4% over the past 60 days. When that gap was above 3%, SPY's next 60 days averaged +4.3% (2004–2014) and +5.8% (2015–2026), against +1.7% and +3.0% for all days.

Put together, this looks like a rotation out of the crowded AI and semiconductor trade that the rest of the market is absorbing, not a market-wide liquidation. That reading has tended to pay over the following three months. It has not protected the next few weeks.

What to watch

· The thrust day's low on a closing basis: 6,992 on the futures. In the past, two weeks of closes above it put this in the stronger half of the cases.

· The pre-thrust low: the November 20 close of 6,910 on the SPX (6,935 on the futures). A close under it would put the market in the group that retested the low first; that group still did better than an average day over three months, after a rougher few weeks.

· Breadth: another day with 82% or more of the S&P 500's dollar volume in falling stocks would restart the cluster count. Equal weight continuing to lead would keep the rotation reading intact.

Given that the market structure of lower highs and lower lows remains in place, it opens the door for further losses. The first support is $40.00, followed by the YTD low of $38.20. A breach of the latter will expose $35.00.
